exerci.e prudence before purchasing a dress of this style as the hairs soon rub off and the effect is spoiled by the bare patches, anyone may safely invest in a soft angora felt hat or toque. These felt hats do not require much trimming. A couple of stiff, quills laid flat across the crown and a full rosette of ribbon is enough, or a twist of velvet and some autumn tinted foliage. The smart' toque sketched is of brownish hairy felt, trimmed with a wreath of leaves which shade from dull green to red. The trimming and eache-peigne at the back are of reddish brown ribbon. The effect is a very pleasing one and can be worn with any kind of costume. Another simple method of trimming a hat this season is to take one of those fringed scarves which have been so fashionable of late, particularly on Panama hats, and twist it carelessly round the crown, tied carelessly at one side in a bow, the fringed ends shading the brims or forming part of the eache-peigne behind. Instead of stitching these into place it will be found a much simpler and better plan to purchase a card of ornamental headed pins such as .one can obtain anywhere for two to three pence per dozen, and catch the scarf here and there to the crown or brim just where it is necessary. _ _

The coat and skirt illustrated is of a simple design and yet is altogether up to date, in style. It is of black cloth, and the coat can be worn open or closed. ' The skirt is perfectly plain and is not so voluminous or lengthy as those affected earlier in the year. Basques are fashionable and the most becoming and simple style is here shown. A strapping of bright

'TENN TOILETTE. red velvet finishes the collar and forms the cuffs, while the waist is finished by a black patent leather belt. This makes a really elegant toilette. About five and a half yards of the cloth double width, together with half a yard of velvet cut on the cross would be found sufficient for making a dress of this style. I should suggest for wear underneath the coat a shirt blouse of soft silk of a bright red shade spotted with white, finished at the throat by a/dainty little turn-over collar of lace-edged lawn and a smartly tied black satin scarf. The black felt hat should have a crown of black velvet and at the back a bow and cache-J;(4oe of fonlard ribbon patterned in a conventional design.

A very smart little coat forms the subject of the third sketch. This ft-made of light brown cloth and has a high fur collar and revers of fur. It is double-breasted, the front being ornamented by groups of little ornamental buttons. A muff to match is worn and a dainty collar and jabot of lace finishes the throat. div.head: 'THE NEXT STAGE IN THE EDUCATION FIGHT.
div.p: 'THE NEXT STAGE IN THE EDUCATION FIGHT.
A CHAT WITH THE REV. THOMAS LA*
The Education fight is entering on a new stage. The Free Church Councils throughout England and Wales have sent in their votes as to the general, enrolment. of the names and
address e; of those who feel that they are bound to refuse payment of the rates levied under the Bill if it should become law. .The

replies have been considered by the General Committee of the National Council. With a view of learning what is to be the next step in the campaign, I managed to secure a few minutes chat with the Re-v. Thomas Law, the General Secretary of the National Council. "I suppose, Mr. Law, I shall be about the 999th interviewer that you have seen lately," I remarked as I was ushered into his private office.

"Not quite that," answered Mr. Law, with a smile; "though you Press men have seemed to regard me as your lawful prey lately; still, I am not disposed to grumble, fore you have helped us nobly in this great Education fight. The newspaper reports of our public meetings, and of the speeches of our leaders, has opened the eyes of hundreds of people whom the five million leaflets we have circulated, and all our public demonstrations,- could never have reached." "Well, Mr. Law, please look upon me as also wanting to help you, and tell me what is to be the next step in the campaign?" "Before doing that," said Mr. Law, "it is desirable I should in a sentence or two outline what we have done. This is necessary that your readers ifiay clearly understand the present position. The campaign began, as you may remember, with a great Conference at St.. James's Hall on April -IZith, at which repre- sentatives were present from all parts of England and Wales. This Conference unanimously determined resolutely to oppose the Government Bill. The day after the Con- ference an influential deputation waited on Sir Henry Campbell - Bannerman, who expressed himself in full sympathy with the object of the deputation, and was quite pre- pared vigorously to oppose ,the Bill in the House of Commons. The Education Com- mittee of the National Council at once took action. Meetings were organised in hundreds of towns. Thousands of personal letters expressing disapproval of the Bill were sent to Members of Parliament from influential electors in their constituencies. Eight leaflets dealing with the different phases of the Bill were issued, and circulated by the million. A little later a large and influential deputation from the National Council waited on Mr. Balfour at the House of Commons. The address then read to Mr. Balfour was after- wards sent to every Member of Parliament, and has since been circulated in tens of thousands all over the land as a manifesto. We have also urged the Council to memorialise their representatives in Parlia- ment, and large numbers of petition-forms have been supplied to every part of the • country. A cia-y of National United Prayer was observed on July 13th, and many other efforts have been put forth. You see, there, fore," continued Mr. Law, "what could be done has been done." "How did this Anti-rate campaign spring into such prominence, Mr. Law?" "Mr. George White, M.P., a' member of our General Committee, and one of our staunchest supporters, was the first public man to give voice to the determination, that has since proved to have been shared by hundreds of people in all parts of England and Wales. Free Churchmen all over the country hailed Ms. White's declaration with enthusiasm, and in a few days the cry was being echoed from hundreds of platforms and in scores of news- papers." "And how came the National Council to be mixed up in it, Mr. Law, for surely it is a skerious thing in a country where law is the only guarantee of freedom to stir up citizens against it ?_" _

"a As to the first portion of your questics," was the reply, "you must know that the National Council is the recognised national organisation of all the Evangelical Free Churches. This Education question is one on which Free Churchmen of all denomina-

-Lions felt deeply, and they naturally turned to us to give expression to what so closely affected them. If you think there has been any agitation to arouse opposition to the law of the country you are entirely mistaken. Free Churchmen have proved over and over again that they are the staunchest of law abiding citizens. But," continued Mr. Law, reflectively, "there is such a thing as conscience, you know, and when that speaks there is no alternative for us but im- plicit obedience, even at the risk of the spoil- ing of our goods." "But do you think, Mr. Law, that any great -number of people feel so keenly on the matter that they will risk prosecution rather than pay the rate?" I asked.

"I know there are," was the decisive reply. "We have just received ample proof of it. For some time a great number of representative -men throughout the country have been urging vs to pronounce in favour of the non-payment of rates. We felt the gravity of such a step to be so great that we could not do so until we had received an expression of opinion from our local councils. Therefore, on August 22nd we sent a circular to the councils giving the pros and cons of the question, and asking them to vote for or against an anti-rate campaign. The result has been most remarkable and sig- nificant. rp to the present 489 councils have voted, of these 29 were against a campaign and 412 in favour, 48 remaining). neutral. That is surely a complete answer to your question?" "It is, Mr. Law, and so I suppose.your Coun- cil will now voice publicly this conscientious feeling?"

"That is so," was the reply. "But let me be quite clear. We do not feel this is a mat- ter of machinery." "Do you propose further approaching the Government before Parliament re-assembles on October 16th Mr. Law?" I enquired.

"Yes," was the answer. "At the largely at- tended meeting of our General Committee on Monday it was decided that we should restate our position to the Prime Minister, and give liim the figures I have just given yob, so that he may see the extent of genuine feel- ing there is in the country." "What other forms will your opposition take during the autumn and winter, supposing, of yours°, that the Bill is not withdrawn?" s "Well," answered Mr. Law, "we shall fight lortaciously the municipal elections in Novem- iser. I have this week signed a circular, along with Mr. S. Woods, M.P., Secretary of the Trades Union Congress, and Mr. A. J. Nundella, Secretary of the National Education Itssociation, to be issued to municipal electors, urging that every candidate should be pledged to support the Withdrawal of the Education Bill, and to vote against the granting of public money to schools without public control. This is entirely a non-party political campaign. Let me repeat here to to-3e who intend nominating candidates that the official nomination will be received by each Town Clerk before 5 p.m. oifFriday, the 24th inst. I emphasise this so that our friends may see there is no time to lose in exerting their influence."

"And are your public meetings in the coun- -17 continuing, Mr. Law?" I asked, preparing depart as the ring of the telephone reminded Me that others were waiting to see the &ere- 'hwy. 'Tea," answered Mr. Law, as he shook hands, °the number of meetings—citizens' and towns' A:l.e etings, as well as Free Church demonstra- tions—increases. We have concentrated our energy mainly on October and November, and ter plan includes hundreds of towns from Am- wick to to Penzance, and shows that the tide of imbijo feeling on this question is steadily :b- -iog.*

autumn the collar—is-eith- e-r-a---very large and pro. flounced feature or is conspicuous for its total absence. Of course, if one is the possessor of a handsome necklet of fur, the latter is certainly the style to be preferred, as it is much more comfortable and prevents the fur from getting rubbed. Still, there is something very be- coming and cosy-looking about a high rolling collar of fur, which protects the back of the neck from all draughts and forms a soft look- ing frame to the face. Coat sleeves are being cut very wide and full near the hands, where they either fall open to show an undersleeve or are caught into a band. Some of those which are kimono or bell-shaped are finished off by tags or tassels at the outside of the cuff. A novel design in coat sleeves shows the sleeve shaped outwards from the elbow to the wrist where It is fashioned into a cuff which has a deep point coming well down over. the back of the hand. Indeed, it is in the fashioning of the sleeve that fashion evinces mott origlnality, and plenty of scope is given for' the exercise of individual taste,

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY OCTOBER 10 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY OCTOBER 10 1902
WOMEN'S CHAT.

Extensive preparations are being made for the Royal progress through London on October 25t.b. On that cecasion, their Majesties the King and Queen will drive in the new State leaden, which was specially built for the abandoned Coronation precession. It is a splendid looking carriage; upholstered in crimson satin and lace, aid it has a more rraceful appearance than most State vehicles, as it has no coachan'e box or bammercloth. Its moulded iplasher is of crimson patent leather, sod with its massive brass lamps and Its deaoration in the Royal colours, the carriage altogether presents a very handsome appearance. It will be the first time that such a State carriage has been seen in public for very many years. as the landaus used by Queen Victoria in both of the Jubilee preoessions, were only of the fetal- State variety. Many of the noble families boast a State coach, and Lord Selisburyl, after those belonging to Royalty,is one of the handsomest of these gerrous specimens of the roach builder's art. That too, belonging to the Duke of Marlborough, fully accords with the ambition of the Maltese to keep up the Marlborough traditions in all their ancient glory and splendour. The Duke of West- minster's, is scarcely so grand, eves though the Gresvenors are by far the richest of the dukes, even with the Vanderbilt wealth thrown in. One objection to auoh vehieles is, that the splendour of the etsaeh is liable to make the occupants appear less distinguished looking, but this cannot be said of the Duchess of Westminster, er of Lady Londonderry, or Lady Lanedowne,when they go abroad in their state carriages. Soeiety it Seems was recently scandalised in a certain rural distriet by the minister of the parish turning out, like any ordinary labourer, to do a week's harvesting. One does net envy the mind that eould see anything I derogatory in such a proceeding, as it would seem to all but the aarzere minded to be an example which many of the black-coated class might follow with advan- tage to their health,and the benefit of the community. Farmers, in their generally straitened eircumstaners, are compelled to work short-handed, and they are invari- ably ia need of assistance at harvest time. The days of the 't jolly farmer " however, seem pest beyend recall, , and with him has disappeared that great social event in the country—the Harvest Flom'. It used to leo one of the meet picturesque of rural euctemr, but aewadays it is practically extinct There is scarcely a Royal family 'in Europe for which the famous firm of Wedgwood in the Staffordshire Potteries has not executed orders, and in spits of all we hear of American pre-eminence, Mrs Roosevelt has recently besome a customer of the firm, for a tea, dinner and desert service. The services comprise altogether 1,296 pieties, the ware being of plain white background with a gold rine,and the United States Arms on each piece. It says a good deal for English art pottery that the order has passed to this country, not- withstanding the competition of German firms. Both the Freaoh and the Germans had made considerable progress in this industry, before needern art pottery was so greatly advanced in this country byJesials Wedgwood in the eighteenth oeatury. Much trouble and annoyance would be saved if we could obtain good glassware which servants could not I break. Many years ago a toughened, or unbreakable kind wax brought out, lout for some or other reason it never came Into general use. Muria is now hoped for from a new process of producing asallisble glass, which has none of the drawbacks of brittleness, and it is said that a lamp chimney made of it may be taken hot from the dame, and plunged into icy oold water without harm. It can be made so tough that It can be used as a banner, and it can also be manufactured into the thinnest table ware, which may be handled with safety, even by the most careless. As a rule the cost of renew. hg glassware in general use is no inceneiderabie item in the household, and it wenlsi be a great advantage if we could sabstitute an unbreakable kind for that which is constantly needing to grief somehow or other. o veiled are the new shapes in millinery that it ought not to be a diffietilt task to suit every style of face. There he the high-crowned bat, which reminds one of nothing is mush as the Welshwoman' typical headgear. Then there is the Toreador, largo, round, and flat, with its broad upturned brim hung with fringe, or trimmed with a fall of lase, which finishes in the long-flowing osohs-peign. The only other trimming eriesessary is a twist of velvet to raise it at the bask. Velvet is being greatly used by milliners, both as a trimming and for , covering the centre shape. It is a very becoming fabric ' but not an easy one te keep free from dust, and then there is the ever-present risk of spotting with rain. The !egg-haired felts are certainly le m becoming, but they , are much better wearing, a consideration when ecteaoray has to be the order of the day. . .

When ehoesing velvet for a togas or hat, eare should hC taken that it is at least two er three shades darker than the falario at the gown, with whioh it ie intended to be dented. Velvet takes Buell high lights, that the FIRMS shade, when worn, at:mars nf nv,•h lighter tone. Broadly 'peaking, far a blonde,tke most charming colour is sapphire Warp, for the brunette brown, but the latter must be a shade as so darker than the hair upon which it rote. _

Very dainty are some of Um specimens of mask weer, in evidence, the majority being of the collar and tie order. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL,
BY G. B. BURGIN,
(Author of "A Quaker Girl," ctc.)

PART IV. Isabel sat up in bed, her long hair breaking from its bonds and flowing loosely around her. She drew it through her fingers, and the soft glossy mass calmed her troubled nerves. It had the effect of a comforting hand in the semi-darkness of the par- tially-lighted room. But after a time, the old disquiet returned. She was as wide awake as if she had been experimenting with Jerome's German bed. Pillow, sheets, everything, appeared to want to climb into the wrong places. Perhaps it was her own restlessness which had thus imbued inani- mate objects with life. The bed had the effect of being filled with crumbs, and most of us knosi, that painful and unpleasant experience. Presently, the ghosts in the distant corners of the room became insupportable. The cloak on the chair sat up, talking to them in noiseless whispers. These unbidden guests appeared to be enjoying themselves hugely at this unholy hour of the morn. Isabel felt seriously annoyed with herself, but it was really no use. She could not sleep. How, could she remedy this disastrous state of things? Suddenly she smiled. "I have it " she said, protruding an ivory foot in the moonlight. "Now, you grim goblins, I'll banish you to any other place I can think of. lam not going to have my apart- ment tenanted by such an unholy crew of phantasms and irresponsible shapes." She got out of bed, and glided across to the cloak with a sigh of relief. It was a warm one. She put it on, and sank back in the easy depths of the chair; but the moonlight still troubled her, and she had not sufficient energy to alter the blinds so as to shut it out. She dozed uncomfortably for a little while in the chair, and they pushed it back into the dark corner of the room supposed to be inhabited by the ghosts which had mocked her attempts at sleep. With the aid of her dressing-gown and a soft cushion, Isabel made herself comfortable in the cosy old chair. She felt very pleased to have escaped from the thraldom of her gloomy couch. To- morrow—or wasn't to-day to-morrow, seeing that it was three o'clock ?—she would speak to Miss Summerby about it, and have something more modern substituted for this hearse-like structure. She leaned back with half-shut eyes. As she did so the bed assumed to her-the proportions of a stage. Little sprightly forms strutted about the coverlet. She could not avoid thinking what a capital place it would make for a meeting between Oberon and Titania. The gloomy curtains would do for the forest trees, and the celoured coverlet might, for the nonce, represent a fairy ring. She had been wide awake before ; all at once she became trebly so. A shiver ran through her. The chair was not so comfortable as she had expected. She would arrange the blinds and go back to bed again. list! What • was that? Oh, Heaven ! what. was that? There was a slight creaking of the door—some- thing in white glided into the room. • Was it really Lady Mary at last? But-no I This ghost had a head. The face was turned from her as it glided slowly,towards the bed. Something glistened for a moment in the moonlight, descended on the bed, there was a rending of linen, and then this ghastly figure drew back the'-bright blade only to strike and strike again with savage fury at the place where Isabel ought to have been. Isabel was not a coward, but at the sight of this figure striking with noiseless fury at the bed she gave a penetrating shriek and became un- conscious. When- she recovered consciousness she was alone on the floor. She fancied that she heard Geoffrey Hearne's Lvoice outside theihouse giving instruc- tions to someone in firm, decided tones. She staggered to the, door, locked it,' and again fainted. • Presently someone knocked. "It's only me, miss," said Pilbeam's pleasant voice. "Is anything the matter?" Isabel opened the door, and, flinging herself into the broad, motherly arms of Mrs. Pilbeam, burst into tears. Mrs. I'ilbeam drew her into the room, and shut the door. "There, there, my pretty, my pretty, don't take on so, don't take on 80. Shsll, 8113 h " She rocked Isabel in her strong arms until the frightened girl's sobs gradually subsided, and she was able to give an incoherent 'account of what had happened. "Bless you, my pretty," said Mrs. Pilbeam. "Didn't I tell you what would come of having those late suppers? I oughtn't to have told you about Lady Mary and all that silly nonsense. I might have known you, too, would have lost your head, my pretty one, my lamb." She held Isabel very tightly in her motherly arms. "I warrant me, my pretty, you forgot to lock your door last night, and then you got to dreaming and rememberidg it in your dreams, and fancied all sorts of things. Whenever Kinipple has tasted cheese for supper he does the same thing, my pretty ; " but she gave a shiver as if she did not believe her own account of what had happened. Isabel sat up, and released herself from Mrs. Pilbeanrs strong arms. "That is all nonsense," she said, a little ashamed of her emotion. She glided to the window and opened the blind. The stable clock struck five. "It was too real," shivered Isabel, "too horribly real to be a dream." She rushed to the bed and lifted up the eoverlet. "See here ! see here!" she cried, holding it out hysterically to Pilbeans. "Now tell'me if it was a dream !" The coverlet was pierced, with long slanting slits, in four places. By a strong effort Isabel prevented herself from again fainting. She felt sick and worn out with the emotions of the night. After a moment's interval, she fell on her knees and thanked God that she had been spared. .Mrs. Pilbeam was wimpering by her side. "It's true enough, miss. Heaven forgive me for telling you such a lie. Oh, yes, it's true enough. But I told you to lock your door every night. If you had listened to me you would have been spared all this." "Who was it, then?" inquired Isabel in a frightened whisper. " It was one of the maids, who gets a bit queer in her head at times," said Mrs. Pilbeam. "I can't persuade Miss Summerby to send her away altogether. She gets these fits when the moon is. at full, and that was why I told you to lock your door. You didn't see her face, miss?" " No ; it was turned away from me," said Isabel, not noticing Pilbeath's look of relief. "She seemed to be rather tall and muscular, to judge from the way in which she struck the coverlet." "You had better come with me to my room, miss," said Pilbeam. "You can't go back to that bed again." "I should have a fit if I did," saidDrabel, cling- ing to Pilbeam, gratefully. "Oh, it is so horrid. If I hadn't felt uneasy and gone to sleep in the chair, she would have killed me." "Oh, that was it, miss," said Pilbeam. "I was wondering how it all happened." "Weren't you afraid ?" asked Isabel. "Me afraid !" said the brawny Pilbeam, scorn- fully baring her magnificent arm. "Why I could knock down a man as soon as look at him, and Kinipple knows it, bless you." Mrs. Pilbeam put Isabel to bed in her own coin- fortable room and remained with her until she fell into a troubled sleep. Then she noiselessly left the room, softly opened the front door, and made her way to the tower. Geoffrey Hearne awaited her coming. He was very pale and stern. "'Do you know what you have done, woman?" he said. "It is only by God's mercy that poor girl escaped. You are unworthy of such a trust. How dare you sleep at your post?" Pilbeam whimpered, "It's very hard on me, Mr. Geoffrey. I have not been to sleep for two nights with her, and she seemed so much better that j just dozed off. When I woke up she was gone." "And then?" "I rushed round looking for her. I saw Miss Archer's door open, and she—" Geoffrey grew paler still. " she was stabbing at the bedclothes. I rushed forward, and dragged her away. Miss Archer had fainted on the floor. She couldn't sleep, and so had gone to the other end of the room." There came a groan, and then a sound of low shackling laughter from the room above. "Does Miss Archer susoect anything ? "
"Bless you, no, sir. She thitlke ir one of the inside."

"It is about time this deception ended. I was a fool and a knave ever to consent to its beginning," said Geoffrey. "Ii anything had happened to Miss archer I would have shot myself. I will tell her soon. But you—l trusted you, and you betrayed that trust."

"I'm mortal sorry, sir," said Pilbeam, again weeping. "I didn't feel very well last night, so I swallowed half a tame Indian (presumably, Tamar Indien), and that kept me awake for a time. Then I went to sleep, and she got up." Geoffrey sighed heavily. "It is hopeless," he said. "There is nothing more to be done with her. The whole business must come to an end. I ought to have known better than to have embarked on so fool-hardy an Again that maniacal chuckle. Then all was still.

"She's gone to sleep now, sir," said Pilbeam. "I'll take her back to her own room to-morrow sight." And she went away, leaving Geoffrey buried in deep thought. The next day Pilbeam entered the breakfast- room with a message for Isabel that Miss Sum- merby was too unwell to see any one, and she did not wish to be disturbed. Isabel was to attend to everything until Miss Sununerby felt well enough to do so herself.

Geoffrey Hearne looked up for a moment when the message was given to Isabel, but quickly buried himself behind th 4 Times before she could catch his eyes. She was pale and dispirited. The experiences of last night had been altogether too much for her. She had almost resolved to return home. Hence, Miss Summerby's illness was an additional aggravation'of her perplexities. Geoffrey Hearne, too, seemed strangely preoccupied and ill at ease.

Isabel put aside her untasted toast, and rose to leave the table. She spent the morning in her own room. In the afternoon, several people were closeted with Geoffrey Hearne. "You have no hesitation in signing the certi- ficate," she heard one say to the other' as they left the house, and then it flashed across her troubled mind that these men were doctors who had come to see the mad housemaid, and certify that she really was insane. "If you please, miss, Mr. Hearne would like to see you," said Pilbeam, about four o'clock. Isabel went listlessly down to the study, feeling that something unusual had happened. Geoffrey plired in her hand a telegram. "Would you do me the favour to read that ?" he said.

"I don't understand," said Isabel. " Have full permission to explain everything to Miss Archer. The evil day cannot be put off—Dabchick.' What does it all mean, Mr. Hearne ?" "It means—oh, you must see what it means," he said, driven out' of his usual reserve by her evident listlessness. "Don't you really see what it all means ?"

"No," said Isabel, listlessly. "lam only aware that I am very tired, and that it is not like you to trouble me. I had a kind of feeling that you would protect me, and now—Oh, that horrible woman! I see her now. I hear the rending of linen as she strikes the bed again. lam a coward. I want to go away. I cannot stop in this dreadful place. I knew when I first saw it something terrible would happen. Life seems to have nothing but sorrow for me at every turn. A little while ago, I did not know the meaning of the word, and now—" i She buried her face n her hands, and wept afresh. _

............. Geoffrey allowed her to weep unrestrainedly for a few moments. Then he came round, took her hand in his own, and sat down opposite her. "Listen to me a moment, please, Miss Archer. It is absolutely essential that you heed what I am about to say to you. Isabel stayed her tears. She was very tired. The excitement of the night had been too much for her.

"You will think me a silly school girl," she "I, who boasted of my strong nerves." There was something reassuring in the touch of Geoffrey's hand. She felt more composed. "I have something very painful to tell you," he said. "Can you guess what it is?" "If it is the mystery of this place, I do not want to hear it," said Isabel. "The shock of last night has quite cured my folly about it. All I wish to do is to leave here as soon as possible." "But, in justice to myself, I cannot let you go without explainin how it was that you came here as well as myself," he said. "Do you mind going back with me a year ago?" Isabel nodded. She had not the slightest interest in the mattee. She wanted to leave the place. Geoffrey said nothing for a moment. "Prepare yourself for a shock," he resumed. "The mad woman who entered your room last night was not a servant at all. It was Miss Suramerby." "And you knew it!" said Isabel, her listlessness vanishing. "Yes. "How did you know it?" "Because," said Geoffrey Hearne, drawing his hand away, "I am her keeper." "Would you mind telling me all about it?" said Isabel, incredulously. "What harm had I -ever done to Miss Summerby that she should try to kill me ? " -

" About a year ago," said Geoffrey, "my poor dad lost all his money. The old place had to be sold—the sho.ik killed 'aim. I was the only son— the young squire. ' A young squire whose property has gone to pay his father's debts is not of much account in the world, as I speedily found out. I could do nothing—l was perfectly useless, except as a gainekecper. I came to town, and almost starved in my attempt to make a living. One day I saw a curiously-worded advertisement in the _ Daily Chronicle. It said that none but gentlemen need apply, and that, after a preliminary interview, if the applicant suited, the nature of the post to be filled would be disclosed. I went to the address, and saw--"

"Mr. Dabehiek," said Isahel, eagerly. "Yes, He looked nic over, and thought that I I should do, but he was very particular as to my antecedents—wanted to know all about me, in fact. I was to return to him in a week's time. He would then, if I suited, fully disclose the nature of the post to be filled. I went back in a week's time. I daresay you know the place. He said he had been down to my home to make inquiries about me. He had even called on the vicar, whose name I had given as a reference. At first I felt inclined to choke him for his impertinence. • But I am tiring you ?" "Not at all," said Isabel. "I want to know everything." "He then disclosed to me that it would be a very easy place for me to fill. You will be called an agent,' he said, and will have a capital horse and quarters. You will live with an old lady in Derby- shire, who came into a large estate a short time :back. I am one of the trustees of the will by which she inherits. She has one or two distant relatives; in the event of anything happening to her, the money goes to a hospital. lam afraid something will happen to her. The shock of coming into this largo fortune after a life of com- parative poverty has been too much for her. I don't think she will ever get over it. The doctors laughed at me when I mentioned my doubts, but I told them I had never seen a person stick out her thumbs at right angles, and make no use of them, who did not go mad in time. It was only a ques- tion of time. And the madness generally took the form of homicidal mania. They laughed, but they examined Miss Summerby—that is her name— without her knowledge. Then they came to me with long faces. There were•grave signs of mental disorder. They didn't believe in my theory about humbs, but it was just a toss up whether Miss Summerby would go mad or recover. She needed incessant watching, but she must not know it. If she onoe became aware of her danger, she would inevitably go mad. All they could suggest was that her female attendant should be a woman accus. tomed to the care of the insane."
"Then Pilbeam has been a keeper?" asked Isabel.

"And is. That accounts for her extraordinary strength. Dabchick said that there must always be a man on the premises in case of any outbreak. It would not be sudden. Some hours would elapse in any case, but it needed someone to be always on the look out for the symptoms in Question. It

"That is why I was selected?" asked Isabel. "Yes. Dabchick prides himself on his know- ledge of character. He thought it would be better not to tell you the truth. He told the girl who was here before, and she became so nervous that she frightened Miss Summerby into a bad attack about four months ago. She went away, and Miss Summerby began to mope. You did her a great deal of good. Sometimes you have looked very surprised when I have asked you to go on playing. You didn't know that you were playing the evil atirit out of this kindly. old lady, who would not Willingly hurt a fly. She is naturally one of the gentlest, sweetest souls living, and I have had' to take her screaming, struggling to the Tower—one stores is padded—and keep her there for hours, poor soul, until the madness is passed away. I was beginning to hope that she would recover, but .Pilbeam told me she was becoming restless again. That was why I didn't want her to go for a drive, but I couldn't very well stop her. She has never been as bad as this. It was Pilbeam's duty to sit up with her, and to call me if she became worse. It seems that Pilbeam went to sleep. A soldier who goes to sleep on duty is shot. If anything had happened to you, that woman ought to have been shot. She went to sleep, and was only just in time to prevent Miss Summerby from attacking you as you lay unconscious. Miss Summerby had snatched a knife from a drawer. You know the rest. Pilbeam managed to secure her, and called me. I brought her into the padded room. She is there now."
"It is horrible, horrible 1" said Isabel, "I am glad to think, poor soul, that my music cheered her up. If I had been kinder, perhaps she would never have become ill."

" She took a great liking to you," said Geoffrey. "Mad people always strive to kill their dearest friends. I don't know how it is, but the fact remains. I telegraphed to Dabchick this morning; you see ,his reply. The doctors confirm his view of the case.- She will be taken away to-night—taken away to an asylum, there to end her days. She has been good, kind, merciful to those around her, and yet in her old age there ip no mercy shown to her. She must go. Heaven watch over, and com- fort her, for she has comforted many." He spoke very solemnly. It was easy to see that he was deeply moved. "And you?" asked Isabel, "what will you do?"

"I?" he said. "Oh, don't think of me at such a time as this. I shall go abroad to the Diamond Fields. I have a chum out there who has often urged me to do so. I had already written to Dabchick to say that he must find someone to replace me' and that he has no right to expose you to any risks. was only waiting until you had learned the truth, to see how you would take it, and then I was prepared to go.' "You were ever thoughtful of my happiness," said Isabel, in faltering tones. "I seem to have known you all my life. I—l cannot bear to think of your going forth into the world like that. And I owe my life to you also. What can I give you in return ? "

"Dear," he said, softly, "I fear I have learned to love you more than anyone else. But now I have no right to speak." And he turned away. "Stop," said Isabel, placing her hand upon his coat. "Stop, you have already said too much, or--" She hesitated. "Or what?" "Not enough." . . . . .
- He took her hands in his.

"I have a confession to make, and—and to ask your forgiveness." "Wait until you have heard my story," said Isabel. "Do you know that I was despi.ed and rejected by my lover because I had no money? That he taught me to love him, and then, when all the world expected him to speak, he went away in silence."

"I know all about it," he said. "I heard the story from Dabehiek. That was why I horse- whipped Deep, and made him speak out under a penalty of another thrashing." "You did that?" she asked. "You horse- whipped_ him and then sent him to propose to me. Why?" "Because I could see that you had loved him, and I wished to know for myself whether you still did so. That was why." "Was that all?"

"No," coming a step nearer to her," it is not all. I loved you myself from the first moment I saw you. I could see that you had received a shock. When I found out what it was I resolved to help you. Deep should speak out. You made your choice, and refused him." "Do you know why I did so?" she asked. "No.' "Because," she said, excitedly, "I found out for myself the difference between the false and the true. I came here wretched, heart-broken, too poor in self-respect to lift my head. You watched over me, healed my wounds so gently and unobtru- sively, that I scarcely knew it at first. Then I thanked God that he had opened my eyes in time, and also thanked Him "—her voice sank to a low, sweet whisper—" for—for you." Geoffrey's hand shook a little as he lifted it from the back of the chair.
"To-morrow we go our diverse ways." "Yes, to-morrow," she said, "but my heart will be with you until--" "Until I come to claim it," he said. _
Then they kissed and parted, each knowing that in God's own time that morrow will purely come. __

And so the House on the Hill gave up its secret in the silvery moonlight. One tragedy more ox less, what did it matter? Reason, love, life, death were only passing phases of the pigmies who sought shelter within its ancient walls. Others would come and pass away like sunlight on the water, and-this ancient house remain. Let them go!

For the past six months deceased had been drink- ing heavily and had also been strange in his manner. but witness had never heard hi ra threaten to take away his life.—fhomas Spencer, • tanner living at 7, Beck Crossley-street said that at 12.15 on Thurs- day last he went to an outbuilding adjoining the house and found the door shut. div.head: PLUCKY DEED REWARDED. A London Benefactress to a Warrington Bootblack.
div.p: A PLUCKY DEED REWARDED. A London Benefactress to a Warrington Bootblack.

The plucky action of Albert Harrison, a cripple, awka follows the occupation of a bootblack, and who reamed a boy named Walter Goodson, aged mix years, residing in Ernest-street, from drowning in the Sankey and St. Helens Canal at Buttermilk Bridge, eon Sunday, September 13th, last week obtained tangible recognition from an unexpected eeuree. It will be remembered that Goodson was playing on the canal bank with several companions when he overbalanced himself and fell into the Water. Harrison, who happened to be near, took off his overcoat and jacket and lay down on the bank. With the assistance of his crutches he suc- ceeded in pulling the boy out of the water, and after wrapping him in his overcoat took him home te his parents. A paragraph recording the event appeared in the " Daily Mail " and last Saturday the Chief Constable (Mr Luke Tallapt) received a letter from the correspond- ing editor of Ihac paper, stating that a cheque had been sent to the proprietors for the henefit of Albert Harrison, and asking if he would investigate the case. The Chief Constable, after making inquiries, replied to the effect the.; the facts were as reported, and that if the cheque were gent payable to him he would cause the money to be handed to Harrison and obtain his re- ceipt. On Tuesday Mr Talbot received a cheque value £9 8s from the newspaper proprietors,together with the letter written to them by the correspondent who had forwarded the cheque. The letter was from a lady who resides in Ormand Mansions, one of the most fashion- able neighbourhoods in the West End of London. It appears that be had read the " Daily Mail "paragraph whilst staying at Boulogne-snr-Merg in France, and had interested her friends who were staying at the hotel on Harrison's behalf, with the result that £9 8s was subscribed. On Tuesday the Chief Coestable wrote to the " Daily Mail corresponding editor stating that he had that day handed £9 88 in cash to Harrison and forwarded his receipt for that amount. He added that Harrison was a young man in whom lie had taken a great deal of interest for some time past. He was unfortunately somewhat simple minded as well as being a cripple and was unable therefore to obtain a livelihood in the ordinary fields of industty, hence he was in very straightened circumstances. He (Mr Talbot) had arranged to become temporarily Harrison's banker to the limit of the cheque and to assist in start- ing him in a small green grocery business. Parrison wished to convey through him his very sincere thanks to his benefactress and to the "Daily Mail 'for the hand- some present sent to him. Personally he (Mr Talbot) considered the lacWs action a very noble and well d irected one.

Concert at Winwick Asylum. The other evening Mrs W B Roberts and her ladies' orchestra entertained the inmates and staff of the Asylum with a long programme of vocal and instrumental music. The orchestra played several selections, marches, kc., which were greatly appre- elated, and the audience were delighted with the songs Miss Edith Birchall and Miss Sutton contri- buted. These ladies,in fact,nearly doubled their share of the programme in response to the insistent ap- plause Mr Victor Roberts highly amused the audience with his comic songs and patter, and sang several additional songs in answer to repeated de- mands for more. Tke Misses Sutton, Francomb, Willett, and Wilson, and Messrs Bean, Mier, Sutton and Longdin sang quartette from " Floradora " and the " Silver Slipper," which also were very much enjoyed. Warrington League of the Cross. The members of the above branch of :the League of the Cross have had quite a record week of suc- eeseful events. On Sunday, September 281h,a large number attended to hear a lecture on " Rome" with limelight views by the Rev Father Gibbons, of St Alban', Bewsey-street. The members felt they had bad in the hall. The whole of the members renewed their pledge of total abstinence with Father Gibbons and a good number of new members were enrolled. on Monday, September 29th the annual dance in aid of the League of the Cross Brass Band was held in the Co-operative Hall, Winwick-street and was a great success. Advantage was taken of the spirit brought about by the above events to arrange for the members to go in a body to the silver jubilee opening of St Mary's Catholic Church Buttermarket- street on Sunday October .sth. The members readily consented and at the appointed time 6 o'clock a large number met at the Hall and At 6.10 headed by the brass baud they proceeded to evening service. After service they again formed up and marched back to the hall, Where Mr T Kil- gallon V.P., in a brief speech thanked all those who had taken part in the parade and announced that in honour of the event the manager asked that an extra hour be given to the members for recreation. This was granted. During the evening Mr D Dolan (cornet) and Mr J W Brown (euphonium), rendered some excellent awed solos, which brought a pleas- ant evening to a slime.

At a meeting of the Paving and Rewrap Committee, it was resolved that the Electricity Committee be em- powered to reinstate, by their own workmen, the streets Interfered with by their department, Subject to the statutory *otiose being given to tie Borough Surveyor, and the work executed to his satisfaction. Councillor Trxrtrox. is moving the report of the Pav- ing and Sewerage Committee, said he was serry to state that the health of the chairman of this eemmittee pre- vented his attendance at the Ceuneil that evening. He had had a relapse, and was net at all well. Proceeding, he said they would see by the mistletoe that there were a large number of streets and passages which would be shortly taken in hand at ths expiration of the menses ordering the paving of the same, and they hoped to speedily put the streets in such order that the inhabi- tants would enjoy more comfort and have ne teases to grumble. (Hear, hear). Referring to the recernrseada tion with regard to the Electricity Committee given above, he Said the reason they had done this Was be- Canoe the Paving and Sewerage Committee had had con- siderable reason to grumble at the way in which some of the streets had been re-laid after the work of other committees had been *done. They would remember that at the last meeting of the Electricity Committee he had brought this matter for- ward, and the engineer then said that they were plate prepared to do the re-instatements upon their work after excavation, and that they oeuld do it cheaper than the Paving Committee. The Paving Committee, having me much work to follow up the work of the other com- mittees, thought they could very well give the electricity Committee the opportunity of putting their own work in order. He hoped that they would do the work in a sernewhat different manner to what was being done at the present. He had that day visited Liverpool-road, and had seen the condition of that road. It was a grace and a danger to the berough. The excavation had been left in a very unfinished state, and in.filling up the excavations the filling had been thrown and not put in. Tne footpath from the Ship Ina to the corner of Green-street had been raised from three te five inches ; the tiles ivad not been replaced as they should have been. He supposed that they were leaving it to settle. They were probably going to have very con- siderable trouble, and he could quite sse that somebody

was goiag to have something to pay in the event of an accident there. The same remarks applied to St Mary's- street in Letehford. Be had to complain as to the manner in which the Electricity Committee, the Water Committee and the Gas Committee did their work—er rather the way in which they did not de it. They threw the things together,and naterally everyone looked to the Paving and Sewerage Committee as the responsible committee. It was not very pleasant for the Borough Surveyoe's Department and the Paviiig Committee to feel that other committees were not doing as much as they might to make the work as easy as possible. He hoped that this would be taken and understood as a friendly sort of hint. IC was only fair that the public should understand that the Borough Surveyor and the Paving and Sewerage Committee were not to blame for the state of the streets. Alderman Itureamsoer seconded. In answer to C aancillor Beanett, Counoillor TINNION said they did not require the Tramways Committee to make good toe street after their excavating, because toe Paving and Sewerage Committee had had to do so much work for them and bad a contract with them. It was hadvisable to make any fresh arrangement, Alderman SHAW GREEN said he regretted very much that it was necessary for Mr Councillor Tmnion Co make such a statemeat at that meeting. It seemed to bins that Alderman Dionks' suggestion as to a meeting between committees and olEciele had not been acted up to or it would not have been necessary to make such a state- ment as Councillor fintaion had made. Be did not know how even their reepeneible guides and assistante had met, but be certainly thought it was time they did meet if it was neceesary for such a statement to be made in the Ceuncil. SERVICE TO PADGATE BRIDGE.

A meeting of the Tramways Committee was held on September 10th, when the question of the construction of a tramway to Padgate Bridge was considered and again deferred. The manager reported that the tender of Messrs Milne and Co., accepted at the last meeting was for car jacks only, which had been supplied. Tne following resolutions were adopted : That the tender if Messrs Booth aud Co. for the supply of a bogie at £2l. be accepted; that the tender of Messrs Dutton and Bean for two travelling, jaeke at I 7 4s be aeoepted, if afeer inspection they are found satisfactory ; that the queetion of the construction of additional tremways be brought up for consideration in the month of June neat; and that an application be made to the Board of Trade for their sanction to the opening of the Wilderepool Tramway for public traffic. On the 24th September, the Town Clerk produced a letter and a copy of new ' regulations issued by the Board of Trade with respect to guard wires on tramways, which were referred to Mr I Grirnsdale. Alderman ROBERTS moved the confirmation of the minutes, and alluded to the recent inspection of the tramway service to Stockton Heath. The inspector of the Board of Trade expressed himself very satisfied with the work, especially with the precautions that had been taken to prevent the possibility of any accident occur- ' ring at Wilderepool Crossing. Is a result of the inspec- lien the committee were enab:ed to open the service on

the following day, and he was glad to say that the results had exceeded their expectations considerably. (Hear, hear.) He had no doubt the Wilderspcol service would be the best paying portion of the whole of the services, in spite of the drawbacks. (Hear, hear). He should like to take the opportunity of saving that the ' estimate for the Wildersionol section of £13,550—£10,200 ' permanent way, and £3,350 for Overhead equipment— was considerably in excess of the actual cost. The total cost was £11,707, Be that taking into consideration the capital cost in the first instance, and the satisfactory reeeipts as soon as they got tb a service into operation, the ratepayers should be satisfied they had a property about which no anxiety need be felt as to the future. (Hear, hear.) Alderman ilasuconia seconded. Couacillor BENNETT alluded to the resolution of the committee that " the question of the construction of a tramway to Padgate Bridge was considered and again , deferred." He was sorry that that was the decision of the committee, and he thought it was a mistake on financial grounds, and it was also not giving that con- sideration to the inhabitants of that and ef the town that they deserved. The committee entertained the question of providing tramways to Stockton Heath beyond the boundary of the Borough although consider- able difficulties were involved, including special structural arrangement at the bridge, the purchase of property at Stockton Heath ant eveu yet the matter had not been abandoned, and why Stookton Heath should have a consideration which was not extended to another part of the town was to him vague and unsatisfactory. When a very influential body of ratepayers almost unanimously requested that facilities of the kind he had named should be given, the Town Council were not doing their duty in not suppiying them. Lie hoped the matter had not been deferred for all time' Alderman ROBERTS said the committee had only decided to doter the final decision for a short neriod.The matter had not been abandoned. There were some members of the committee who were unable to come to a decision, but Councillor Bennett might rest assured that what ha wishel to be done was within the bounds of possibility. The minutes were passed.

This Sosiety held its usual interesting meeting on Sunday afternoon last, when there was a good attend- ance. Mr Robins, the teacher of the Mene Bible Class, presided, and spoke upon "Its a Beautiful day." To make a beautiful day many things were necessary, a healthy mind and body. ,Vt hen the heart is bowed down with sorrow, then the beautiful day seems to mock, but when the heart is bright, light and cheerful thou the day seems glorious. Mr Heaton of Manchester was the speaker, aud spoke upon" Sin" its effeet upon indivi- duals and Committees. Mr Eccles and the Secretary took part in the meeting. Mr Payton and Mr Pearson were the organist. The secretary remarked that their objects were to carry out the speakers suggestions, by making the lives of its members bright and cheerful. The face when pure and Godly an be taken as an image of Christ, but when spoiled by sin, can be taken as a Judas.

Concert In Aid of the Infirmary and Dispensary. The members of the Workingmen's Committee of the Infirmary and Dispensary are to be congratul- ated upon the success which attended the annual concert promoted by them in aid of that institu- tion, which took place in the Parr Hall on Saturday • evening. Apart from the laudable object the interesting programme was an inducement to lovers of music to attend, and most parts of the hall were well filled. As usual the major portion of the pro- gramme was entrusted to Mr T Down's orchestra, and the manner in which the various items were presented fully maintained the high reputation which the orchestra has so long onjoyed. There was a careful attention to expression, the general effect produced being very pleasing to the audience mho showed their apprectiation by cordial applause. Or Ti Down discharged the duties of conductor with Lis customary ability. The vocalists were Miss resale Moorhouse (soprano), and Mr Walter Lawley 'tenor). Miss Moorhouse posseeses a very sweet voice of considerable range and mated a favour- , ible impression with her interpretation of "sweet ipirit, hear my prayer." Later on she sang " Poor wandering one " very effectively. Mr Walter Lawley was accorded a hearty encore for his spirit- ed rendering of "Yea ! Let me like a soldier fall," in which his robust voice had ample scope. In response be gave" The sweetest flower that blows' with taste and expression. He had the honour if another recall for a meritorious interpretation of "Take a pair of sparkling eyes," and responded with "When other lips." The humorist was Mr Teddy Whittle, whose songs and patter pleased the audience immensely. Mr W Ii Payton ably supplied the accompenintents.

There is nothing that the old Parliamentarian hates so much as an autumn session: but this year the press of work and the number of necessary measures in hand decided the Government, much against their will, to call Parliament together this month. The Premier's hand was especially forced by the slow progress and unsatisfactory state of the Education Bill, which has had a very chequered career. Last week there was a strong rumour that, like its predecessors, it was to be withdrawn, but this has been strongly denied by Mr. Balfour. Many of the Liberal-Unionists seem to be very discontented with certain clauses, which the promoters look upon as essential to the Bill itself: and in Birmingham, Mr. Chamberlain's own particular preserve, there appears to be a decided split. Anyhow this week Mr. Chamberlain meets his leading constituents on the matter; and a great deal must depend on what attitude he adopts, as he is the most influential man in the party and carries a large section with him. The Opposition are most violently opposed to the whole thing and are determined to do their utmost to turn the Government out on this most con- tentious Bill: and Lord Londonderry, the new Minister for Education, and Mr. A. J. Balfour can scarcely be looking forward to their duties of the coming session, which opens on Thursday neat. There are, also, in addition to very many other things, a - lot of South African, questions to be thrashed out finally: and the- session in every respect bids fair to be a ilvely one. The Irish Party, too, have a lot of grievances up their sleeve and promise to make their presence felt even more than usual. This session is interesting alto, as the practical commencement of Mr. Balfour's Premiership, which was only announced just before the adjournment: and it is a topic of general discussion as to how he will shape. The whole of the new Cabinet, in fact, will be on their mettle in the endeavour to keep their position and infuse a little more vigour into domestic politics, spurred by the results of the most recent el•ctions.

To-day or to-morrow, at the close of the atanceuvres of the Channel fleet under Admiral Wilson, H.M.S. Renown goes into dock to be pre- pared for her voyage to India, to take the King's brother and representative. the Duke of Connaught with the Duchess and their suite, to the grand Coronation durbar. The Renown is one of the handsomest of our battleships with plenty of roomy cabins, so that, with the addition of a single bulkhead, she will be able to provide suitable accommodation for the royal Party: and being of light draught, she is well adapted for the passage through the Suez Canal. When she has refitted and been repaired, she will pick up the Duke and Duchess of Connaught at Genoa on October 30th and proceed with them to Port Said, whence they will journey to Cairo and Assouan to be present at the opening of the great

The runaway marriage of the Duke and Duchess of Manchester just over two years ago is still fresh in the memory of everyone : and la,t yearla baby was born at Kimbolton Cac•tle, but. toting a girl, was not an heir to the peerage and family estates. However, at the end of last week. another baby, a boy this time, was born to the Duke and Duchess at Tanderagee Cattle, their Irish place: and in due course, if he lives, this small sou will succeed to the dukedom nrid entailed property. In the MEllla- time he will be known by the secondary titlea of (Ll6->
THE DUKE AND DUCHESS OF MANCHESTER,.
TO WHOM A SON AND HEIR HAS BEEN BORN.

the Manchester family, and will be by courtesy the Earl of Kimbolton and Lord Mandeville. The former title was made extremely well known by his grandfather, the father of the present peer, who was a familiar figure in all circles of London life and went by the universal nickname of" Kim." The latest addition to the Manchester family will be christened "George" in due course. The present Duke of Manchester's name has been kept pretty well before the public, especially by the financial troubles he became involved in in his younger days: and his mother, Consuelo, Duchess of Man- chester—one of the many Duchesses of Manchester —is very well known in society. She was a Miss Yznaga, an American, and the present Duchess was a Miss Zimmerman, the daughter of Mr. Eugene Zimmerman the Cincinnati railway magnate: sp that the infantile Earl of Kimbolton is three- quarters American, a fact which will, doubtless, be a source of great satisfaction across the "herring pond." Another item of fashionable society news is the marriage of Lord Francis Hope, heir to the dukedom of Newcastle, to his cousin. The fiasco of his first nuptials is still fresh in everyone's mind; and it is only a few days since the decree of his divorce was made absolute. As a divorce Father Black, of the High Church party. have been opposing his marriage in a church, which makes the position a little awkward for his brother, the Duke of Newcastle. who is a leading light amongst the Ritualists. Miss May Yohe, his first wife has already re-married in Buenos Ayres to Mr. Putnam Strong.

Of The Eternal City at His Majesty's it may be said without reservation that in the splendour and unerring taste of the production it reflects the greatest credit on Mr. Beerbohm Tree, who is indeed a past master of the art of staging a play. The scenery in itself is worth going to see; and the stage-management of the big crowds and the big effects is simply marvellous. As to the play, Mr. Hall Caine shares with Miss Marie Corelli the distinction of being either much adipaired or much disliked in his work: and those wIM belong to the former class will go into ecstacies over this high-

From the big circulation of the novel the story is widely known: and it is sufficient to say that the author in adapting it has/adhered very closely to the book, which easily lends itself to dramatisation. However, the parts cannot be considered worthy of the caste, Which is excellent: and the acting in most of the rGles should lay the author under a great obliga- tion to the actors. Indeed, it is a long while since better acting has been seen in London. Mr. Tree, as the bold, bad "Baron Bonelli," is as superbly "made up ".as .nral, and, as always, acts as Mr. Tree with an individuality he cannot sink: but he makes a powerfullar.emier in a preposterous play. Miss Constance Collier, more beautiful than ever, makes a fine "Roma," but is, perhaps, a little overweighted in this highly emotional part. Of the others Mr. Robert Taber, as the revolutionary "Rossi." is splendid tnd convincing : while Mr. Lionel Brough plays most strongly as his friend, and makes a special hit in the great " trial " scene. ne Eternal City was recelved with unstinted applause and is sure to. prove a great finaneia, SIMMS.

February 22nd, 1902. Dear Sir,—lt is with much gratitude I am able to testify to the great relief from pain I have had through taking VITADATIO, For ten years I have not known what It was to rise in the morning free from headache besides internal troubles, for which I was treated in the hospital six years ago. However I obtained no relief, and two years ago I again went Into a hospital and underwent a very serious opera- tion of which the removing of a tumour was only a part. I certainly was a little better for a while,then six months ago the doctor told me I had another tumour forming which ought to be removed. Then I asked myself was life worth living. I felt I oould not face another operation my nerves being corn- pletely wrecked through the previous one. Then a friend told my husband to persuade me to try VITADATIO which I did. Although I think I have had a dozen bottles, few enough to have cured a life- time's pain. lam 25 years of age. I never knew what it was to feel well till I took the VITADATIO. I could not walk any distance without suffering agonies. Bow I can walk 3 miles and feel nothing of it, and did so only last week. My friends are astonished at the change in me, and they say I am like a new woman, I know I feel like one, and if by making this public it will benefit others suffering similarly, you are at liberty to do so as VITADATIO is worth its weight in gold, Yours very gratefully, 46, Madryn-street, Liverpool, S. _
B. CLARK.
