Jo HN- ICZNSIT, Mr. Kensit's Death. little bookseller in Pater'

noster.row, is greater le his death than in his life. The great majority of good Churchmen and Churchwomen have regarded his boisterous career with small satisfaction; hut now he has gained the crown of martyrdom, and there is no doubt that his work will receive a great fillip. Mr. KENSIT'S death is not attributed directlY to the blow which some cowardly antagonist aimed at him in the dark; but the shock to the systera caused the sufferer to succumb. He could not have wished for an end of more distinction. Hs had the aureole of martyrdom round about his head, but with very small privations; he was stay- ing in a city where his following is strongest; the Home Secretary had to be moved to open the prison doors and release the son; and in his last hours the BISHOP or LIVERPOOL was chaplain at the bedside. That is how the narrative will run when Mr KENSIT gets his niche in history. The site of the shop in Paternoster-row, harel bY St Paul's Cathedral, will be more interesting to a section of the community than St Paul's itself. Mr KENSIT will be entered by them in the Church's calendar with St Stephen, and if his family have any administrative ability, they will be able to enlarge the Wycliffe band of preachers and widely extend their propaganda. The movement will probably last until the Church is disestablished. Mr.. KENsir's turbulent proceedings broke harshly on the minds of many who have cherished tender associations with the Church of England. His appearances had for them the rudeness of melodrama when the scene of the action was laid in the sacred buildings themselves. But the people whom Mr. KENSIT desired to impress would not read the Low Church newspapers, and the correspondence columns of most of the daily journals were closed to Mr. KENSIT—the Ritual- istic controversy is too threadbare to allow of much space being given to it in the ordinary course. Mr. KENSIT saw that it was necessary for him to "get into the newspapers," and he took the only course open to him. The public outside a few extreme Protestants would have paid no heed to him unless he created sensations; he therefore despoiled churches of their _images, and he stupe- fied ecclesiastical functionaries by regarding the confirmation of the choice of Bishops as more than a formality. When the official paused for an ob- jection Mr. KENSIT objected. It was thought shockingly indecorous on his part; but so long aS our present system remains an occasional surprise of this sort will occur. Some day, perhaps, even 3 Cathedral Chapter may exercise its conge delire. At present we know that the whole proceeding is a solemn farce. For one thing we may be glad, that Mr. KENsiT,with his remarkable organising ability and personal ambition, was as loyal to the Church of England as he was. His work was not construc-

tive-; and it is only by constructive schemes that men can in their lifetime get glory or fame. The tendency of the age, however, is to give warni • sympathy to any extravagant development in the name of religion. We see it in the support which Christian Scientists are deriving from the wealthY and influential; we see it in the flood of anxious correspondence which fell upon Mr. Pia ax on his Messiah pretension ; it is still more remarkable in the growth of Mr. DCW"E' Zion in America. Mr. DOWIE is, 10 fact, gathering together a large community who, live and move at his behest. He runs a bank

whose security is his note of hand; he conducts lace factories ; and settles the garden-city prob- lem by the letting out of small holdings, for which people are eager to pay extravagant prices in order that they may be within the charmed circle of the spirit of Elijah." He requires from all his followers a tithe of their income, as well as free offerings, and without this regular sacrifice they are told that they cannot hope for the blessing of God. No alcohol or tobacco is allowed on the estate, and attendance at any theatre within or without is forbidden. Instead, the people go to Mr. BOWIE'S temple, listen to the songs of the four-hundred white-robed choir, and watch Mr.

- DOWSE registering notices of " promises to pray," which he is making to applicants. They also find fresh material for faith in the Sequah-like array of crutches and other relics of departed disease. Mr. DDWIE charges nothing for his healing, but takes large tokens of gratitude. He is the first man to utilise the telephone and the phonograph for the multiplication of prayers, We may be glad that " our Mr. KENSIT " was so mild and quiet, as compared with the American iconoclasts.

WE need not credit the Compromise. rumour that Mr. BAL- FOUR has gone to Lord LONDONDERRY to discuss with him the withdrawal of the Education Bill. One does not go to Lord LONDONDERRY to discuss any question oc import- ance ; and, in the second place, if the Government were really to admit its failure at a third attempt to deal with the one important problem which it has to solve Mr. BALFOUR'S Premiership would be at an end. But without giving too much heed to gossip, it is quite obvious that compromise is in the air. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, at Birmingham, is facing an organised revolt among his own con- stituents, convinced Unionists all of them, but Free Churchmen who have still enough of their old Liberalism left in them to detest the Bill with all their hearts. It is not difficult to believe that a Minister who thought the compromise of 1870 too liberal will face the rebels in a mood of sympathy. He proposes to meet them in a secret conference, and to gather from them all the objec- tions that can possibly be urged against the me ure. Mr BALFOUR, who remembers, doubtless what happened when Mr CHAMBERL AIN took to secret conclaves in 1885, may well tremble. Three months ago there were already as many as eighty Unionist members who disliked the Bill. Since then they have met their constituents, and the result is that even Churchmen and Tories like , Colonel BowLEs and Sir CHARLES WELBY have declared their open hostility to it. Sir WILLIAM WALROII D, we know, has promised t urge his colleagues in the Cabinet t made a comproraise,but the suggestion he made was altogether inadequate, He proposes that clergymen of all denominations shall have liberty to enter all elementary schools at will. Now 'it will not at all mollify Liberals, whose objection rests on the simple principle that public control
must go with the grant of public money, to pre- sent Nonconformist pastors with a back-door key to the church schools. Nor does it make the destruction of School Boards more palatable to

suggest an irruption of priests, clergymen, and pastors with their rival doginatisms into the unsec- tarian atmosphere of the old Board Schools. Com- promise onsuch lines as these is impossibla. Mean- time the practical course is to concentrate, on the

joint proposal of the Trade Union Congress, the Free Church Council, and the Education Associa- tion, that a strong majority against the Bill should be returned at the November municipal elections. As Sir HENRY FowLER forcibly put it at Wolver- hampton, the Government, elected on a definite issue of foreign policy, has no moral right to force upon the country a revolutionary scheme whieh has no force of public opinion behind it.

BUT meanwhile, with The National Stake. the denominational battle raging in all its fury, and the whole attention of the nation riveted on ex- ternal questions of management, we run a fearful risk of forgetting that something more that re- ligious liberty and a constitutional principle are at stake. It is a healthy trait in the national life that an injustice should arouse so much vehement protest. One can only hope that when this stumbling-block has been removed some of this enthusiasm will be available foethe cause of edu- cation itself. Education, after all, is not a snore question at issue between church and chapel. That we are miserably be- hind our competitors in America and on the Continent is a truism, but is it quite realised how directly this result is traceable to the parsimony with which we find the funds for the training of our children in the elementary schools Given the building and the apparatos, everythin turns on the teachers. Let us look at a few simple facts about their qualifications. Teachers fall into four classes—(l) the certificated adults who are presumably competent ; (2) ex-pupil teachers who are not certificated, and who usually have failed in their examinations; (3) young women assistants, whose only qualification is that they are over eighteen and have been vaccinated; (4) pupil:

Haldane,too little a Liberal to feel as Hr. Asquith feels, and content to tell us that it is a very good Bill if it could be amended in one or two points. What Mr. Asquith—whose recent speeches, even on the South African question, have been genuine Radical utterances—can be doing in this gallery is a curious puzzle. He tells us that the Government has succeeded in uniting the Liberal party, and that the League, of which he is a Vice-President, has no real differences of opinion on living issues from other Liberals. Why, then, does it exist? lilt is not promoting a rival eet of principles, it can only be serving the interests of a rival clique of leaders.

The Buckley-street P.S.A. has passed a resolu- tion protesting against the running of Sunday trams as it is, in their opinion " detrimental to the welfare of the Christian Churches in Warring- too." This latter appears to us to be an unfortun- ate and easily-disputed phrase to have intro- duced into the resolution. However much objec- tion there may be to Sunday trams on purely Sabbatarian grounds, we fail to see that they detrimentally affect the welfare of the• Christian Churches,but rather otherwise. As we have pointed out previously a tram-service on Suaday enables scores of district residents to attend Divine Service in the town who would otherwise have to stay at home from stress of weather and other inconven- iences. Their attendance carfnot do other than increase the" welfare of the Christian Churches," and it is quite likely that more than one minister .may have cause to look upon the Sunday tram as a blessing—hi disguise may be—but certainly a blessing, to his Church. Even in the afternoon it is quite conceivable that the cars are doing more good than harm by taking people into the fresh air of the country and enabling them to spend the otherwise empty hours in a way healthily and morally beneficial. The protest lacks weight, for whatever other considerations there may be—and we have outlined most of them—there is no doubt that the demand for Sunday trams is stronger than and quite as reasonable as the protest against them. We respect the Buckley-street P.S.A. for its strict observance of religious teaching and regret that its well-meant effort should be so obviously mis- directed and futile.

teach • ers, ct ildren who should be at play and at study, but are forced to save the taxpayer. Now in h Whole teaching staff of the Voluntary Schools there are only 38 per cent, of certifi- cated adult teachers. Under the London School Board the percentage is 81. In all School Boards only 51. Consider what this means Every competent teacher in an English Voluntar School has 30 children under his care. In tye English Board Schools the number is still as high as 76. Even if these teachers were as well trained as in Scotland, where all of them have beon to a training-college, and most of them to a university, it is obvious that this burden of work would be grotesquely excessive. Bat the class of teachers we attract are the men who are willing to accept the average salary of £B3 which as certificated assistant-masters they may expect in the Church Schools, and th 3 women who are willing to sacri- fice themselves for a pittance of £5B. It was said of the ancient Athenians that they cultivated beauty with er..onomy. We cultivate inefficiency with niggardliness. In a generation, unless we mend our ways, our children, in the strong language of Sir Jona- GORST, will be fit only to become the hewers of wood and drawers of water for the world.

Last Sunday night saw the close of the Ray F E Powell's eventful and profitable ministry at St. James' Church. In the short period of four years few men could have done more for the parish of which they were the spiritual head, and at the same time take so deeply intelligent and active an in- terest in the affairs of that larger community—the town in which they lived. Mr Powell was some- what of an anomaly, for in addition to being one of the most devout High Churchmen, he was a Radical Socialist, and never attempted to conceal the nature of his beliefs. There was an honest sincerity about everything Mr Powell said or did, and he at once gained the love and esteem not only of his own parishioners, but of scores of people professing a different faith and holding antagonistic views on other matters. Furthermore he is a man of marked ability and gentlemanly instincts—qualities which he has manifested repeatedly, but never more clearly than in his wordy warfare with Nonconformist and other experts on the education question. The rev. gentleman took up a different attitude from the majority of his fellow-churchmen for he opposed the Bill on the principle that it did not give repre- sentation commensurate with the proposed taxa- tion. On its religious aspect he was equally clear, consistent, and firm, arguing as he did that unsec- tarianism as interpreted by Nonconformists was, to him, a dogma, and just as objectionable in the day school as sectarian teaching was to Dissenters. It was truly said of Mr Powell, at the presenta- tion on Monday evening,that while unswerving in his own beliefs he was tolerant of the opinions of others. This is not always the case with High Churchmen, but, as we said before, Mr. Powell's character is anomalous—and, we say now, one truly admirable. Speaking for Nonconformists, we make bold to say that very many of them re- gret his departure as deeply. as the people of his own parish, with whom they and ourselves—join in wishing him" God speed."

"The custom of public-house treating is now justly hold to be one of the chief causes of intern- perance in Ireland," says the rule card of St Patrick's Anti-Treating League, and the remark applies with equal truth and force to this country also. We have no such league here, but if there is a necessity for such an organisation in the " disthressful country" there is an equal, if not greater, need here. Treating is equally prevalent on the commercial as on the social side of life, and in both cases it often does incalculable harm. Many a young man has ruined a promising com- mercial career through falling a victim to the seductive good-fellowship which he imagines is in- herentin treating. Lord Roberts himself showed his keen appreciation of the dangers of this harm- ful habit by the manifesto he issued at the time our soldiers commenced to return from the/ war. He was in deadly earnest in his request that the goodwill of the public towards the " Tommies " should not be shown by promiscuous treating, and we hope his warning had the effect of deterring some, at least, of those individuals cursed with this false kindness. We should welcome a branch of the Anti-Treating League in England, for it is our firm belief that more can be done for the furthering of temperance in this direction than in any other. The number of total abstainers would increase rapidly once treating came into disfavour, and there can be no question that the anti-treat- ing movement, new though it is, is phenomenally bright with possibilities for temperance.

Shop-assistants all over the country have a good friend in Sir Charles Hake, who visited Warring- ton last week to address a meeting of trade unionists convened by the Warrington Trades and Labour Council. The Shops Bill which he is go- ing to introduce into both Houses of Parliament contains proposals which will do much to amelior- ate the hard lot of the overworked, little-con- sidered,shop-assistants. His object is to get an expression of opinion from Parliament deprecating the unnecessarily long hours worked in shops and emphasizing the desirability of borough and dis- trict councils being authorised to make such regulations in respect to the closing of shops and the limitation of the hours of labour as might seem necessary. It will be a difficult matter to get even the Hou-se of Commons in such a complacent frame of mind that it will adopt the suggested course, but at any rate Sir Charles hopes for,and is fairly confident of,a good division. It is well worth while testing the opinion of the House, for if the condition of shop-assistants is only to be bettered bit by bit the modus operandi for securing the desired end can best be decided upon when the members of Parliament had been carefully sounded. There is, of course, the off- chance that Sir Charles Dilke may achieve success greater than he anticipates and even get Parlia- ment to accept:his Shops Bill, which the Warring- ton L'Trades Council pledged itself to support. It is difficult to see what objections could reason- ably be raised to the Bill, but then a stormy Passage through the Houses of Parliament is always expected for private members' bills. Shop- assistants may, however, calmly leave their case in the hands of Sir Charfes,who will leave no stone cuinetnutrned object to h effect has in viewheprai.seworthy and benefi- -1

A resolution was also carried in favour of direct labour representation in Parliament, by which moans it is hoped to get the law amended in several particulars greatly desired by trades unionists. On this point also Sir Charles Dilks offered some instructive remarks. While admitting that the representation of labour on all local b)dies was desirable, he pointed out that "able representation was much more important than merely getting a majority on a local body." This remark is worthy of emphasis and the most earnest consideration, 1 for it is sometimes the case that trades unionists, in their anxiety to secure representation, put forward a plethora of candidates, many of whom are unsuited for the position to which they aspire. There are plenty of en- lightened men in the ranks of labour, and if the Societies will be firm and bring forward only those who are really capable of adequately representing their fellows they should not have much difficulty

The body which calls itself the "Liberal League" has opened its autumn campaign. The result has Merely been to prove that there is a schism within a schism. Mr. Haldane has been ardently sup- porting the Education Bill, which Mr. Asquith and 81r Henry Fowler have attacked with all their energy, Lord Rosebery appears tO sit on the fence, to astute to throw in his lot with Mr
‘JRACKERS CRISP AND CREAItv
THE EXAMINER FRIDA V OCTOBER 10, 1902

Bill. During the week, meetings have been held denouncing the measure and on the whole, success has attended the demoostrators. The petition against the measure has also been largely signed and will in due course be forwarded to the proper authorities. I believe that a mass meeting will be held at an early date and that some prominent educationalists are expected to speak on the ques- tion. Everything points to the falt that a sturdy opposition against the Bill will be developed.

All honour to the Rev Sidney Morris. Speaking at a meeting the other evening the Rev gentleman boldly declared that if the Bill became law he, for one, should refuse to pay his rate. So Lir this is the first public utterance in Runcorn where a distinct pledge has been made against payment of the rate. Before long Mr Morris will have, it is to be hoped, a sheaf of supporters. The executive Free Church Council intend to at once commence an enrolment of those who will not pay the rate. It will soon be seen who are the' stalwarts" unknown and who the " Weak-kneed."

The current number of the" Co-operative News •' contains a copy of the correspondence from " Gavinian "(Mr J G Fletcher, Woodhouses, Frod- sham), together with an apology for the assertions he had made in reference to " Co-operative Methods," and which he says he is unable to prove.

ience. Be did not know indeed that they had suffered any punishment for having perpetuated this illegality Or so many years,and person- ally he would not mind going down to posterity as having committed an illegal act when it was fraught with such tremendous good as came from these evening schools. (Applause.) Religious matters !dere too thorny a subject to be discussed thore, but in his opinion the Board School had achieved a very great success and it would not be without a pang that ho would see the system abolished. If it were, he only trusted that a better one would be brought into exist- ence and that their successors would be more deter- mined than they had been to see that every girl and boy in Runcorn had a sound education such as would fit him or her for the duties of life. In that case he would be perfectly satisfied and would retire into obscurity perfectly bappy. (Laughter and applause.)

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Runcorn, though they won the game on Satur- day,playea very badly until the last fifteen minutes. Somehow or other the team could not get into their usual stride. On the day's play Brighouse were by far the best team, and more than held their own even in the second half with a man short. Had it not been for Houghton, who pulled the game out of the fire, there would have been an utter collapse. Richardson hardly played with his usual brilli- ancy, and missed more than one pass that would have led to something tangible. At forward play, the Linnets were completely outclassed. Over and over again the visitors got possession and if the backs had been as smart as the front rank a different tale would have been told. Luckily for Runcorn two of the Brighouse Rangers were sent off the field for foul play—one for a deliberate foul, the other for deliberately striking Jones in the face when on the ground. It was , prior to the sending off of the second player that Butterworth scored the equalising point amid a scene of the utmost enthusiasm a few minutes be- fore time. On the whole the team will have to look alive and display more combination if they intend to hold their own. The front rank is especially weak and were it not for our backs Run- corn would be in a sorry plight.

div.head: ----.liip-• VICTORIA-ROAD EVENING CONTINUATION SCHOOL.
div.p: ----.liip-• VICTORIA-ROAD EVENING CON- TINUATION SCHOOL.
Annual Distribution of Prizes.

The Victoria-road evenins continuation school, which is conducted under the Ruucore School Board, was re- opened on Monday evening when the annual distribu- tion of prizes took place. There was a large attendance Mr F J Norman presided, and was accompanied by Miss Pritchard (who presented the prizos), the Rev Father Chambers, and Messrs J Littler, J Pritchard, R Morris, land A Lightburn (depaty clerk to the School Board). Mr J W Lightburn (the clerk) was unable, owing to illness, to be present. Mr Moulton (the headmaster) read the following report :—The session ending 30th April, 1902, was the 12th for the men and boys' department and the 9.12 for the girls. 111 the form !r department the school was opened on 65 evenings, and in the girls' department 47 times. Namber of pupils admitted : Girls 54ernen and boys 107, total 161. Average attendance per evening : Girls 33,.rnen and boys 67,t0tal 100,being the same as in the previous session. As a result of the Cockerton judg- ment the evening schools were placed under the control of South Kensiagton,whose inspectors, Mr J Parry Laws and Mr Fenton, paid two visits.:The report of Mr Parry Laws is as follows :—" This is a useful school doing good work.' The highest possible grant was earned for each subject in both schools. The total grant amounted to £92 9s 7.1, which includes a supplementary grant of £l3 43 3d. Last year the grant earned was £lO7 17s, but as there was a reduction £l9 91 61) tinier Art 17 A of the Code known as the 173 61 limit the total grant payable was £9O 161 61. Is will thus be seen that the kraut received for the past session is an increase of £2 63 Ild over that ot the session preceding. It is satisfactory to report that the MOO'S class which was established by the School Board three years ago. with the object of enabling men whose education has been neglec6ed, to have the oopertuaity of acquiring knowledge, has had another successful sefrion. The average attendance per evening in this department of the Continuation school was 23. It is very pleasing to state that some of the men who were entirely ignorant of the rudimeats of education on joining, can now read and write creditably and have a fair knowledge of arith- metic. Last year a similar class was formed for women. With reference to this, Mrs Willcrass (head mistress) re- ports as follows : " A special feature of the school list year was the formation of a class for women. This was attended fairly well, and it was most encouraging to see the perseverance of the ten members who joined.' The pupils in these two adult classes have the advan- tage of working in separate class rooms entirely apart from the younger pupils. In the examinations in con- nection with the Lancashire and Cheshire Union of In- stitutes the pupils were very successful. The summary of results was as follows :--.Total number examined in arithmetic,commercial correspondence and handwriting, book-keeping, and sick nursing 95. Passes : First class certificate, 32 ; second class;l7 ; second class, no certificate, 11 ; pass, 24 ; total, 84. Mrs Killcross, headmistress, reported upon the girls' department as follows :—This school re-opened on Sep- tember 30th, 1901. The number of scholars admitted during the session was 54. A special feature of the school last year was the formation of a class for women. This was well attended, and it was most encouraging to see the perseverance of the ten members who jellied the class. On March 4th, 1902, a visit was paid to the school by Mr J Parry Laws, U.M. Inspector, who seemed thoroughly satisfied with the work and in his report says :—" This is a useful evening school, doing good work." And the examination held by the Lancashire and Cheshire Un'on Institutes, in March last, nine scholars were presented in arithmetic, five of these gained a first class, and three a second class certificate. Feur scholars were presented hi hand writing and commercial correspond- ence, all of whom secured a second class certificate. Out of the nine girls who entered for the examination in sick-nursing, eight were successful in gaining a pass, and one a second class certificate. Miss Pritchard then distribated the prizes. div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISIRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISIRICT COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of the above Counsil was held on Tuesday at Hutt n).—Present Messrs J Knowles (in the char), J Bolshaw, E Clarke, J Whitl,w, T Darlington, T Bizter, C E Linaker. T Bradford, T Wright, J F Collier,S Woodward, G Pilling, E Bretherton, R Billington, Admiral Jones—Parry, J Mountfield, A guest, J. Spruce, G F Ashton (clerk), W E Hough (assistant clerk), Dr Adams (msdicai officer), J Swinton and W Diggie (surveyors), J Farrington (inspector.)
TUE PROPOSED FLOETING MORTUARY,

Earnest S Inman, general manager to the Weaver Navigation, wrote under date 25th September respect- ing the proposed floating mortuary on the Weaver to the eff oct that one floating mortuary would :not in the opinion of the Trustees meet the case. If a person drowned in the Weaver above Northwich, was found, when the craft was on the Weston Canal,hours would elapse bofore it could be available at the required spot. To be practicable three or four such cults should be stationed at different points along the Navigation. As the Council's care was for the Runcorn district only the trustees would be prepared to find mooring places for such crafts if provided by the Council. Apart from that they regretted their inability to do more and failed to see that there was any call upon them to make provi- sion for drowned persons. Resolved that the Clerk write to the overseers of the parishes enclosing the correspondence with a copy of the Corouer's letter asking could they find provision for such bodies.
THE THELWALL NUISANCE.

The Clerk said that the committee appointed at the last meeting to meet Mr Naylor respecting the Thel wall nuisance duly met.and after discussion had an adjourn- ed meeting at which the surveyor produced a tracing showing how the sewage from the different properties contributing to the pollution of the Thelwall Brook beyond the culvert under the Bridgwater Canal could be collected. It was resolved that the different owners be asked if they are prepared to treat the sewage from their respective premises and so save the parish the cost of an expensive sewage scheme, and that the one foot sewer in Weaste-lane be reconstructed with an eighteen inch pipe. Mr Bradford proposed and Mr Bolshaw seconded the ' adoption of the report. Admiral Jones Parry asked whether the recommenda- tions respecting certain alterations made some weeks ago had been carried out. Mr Swinton replied that all the work had been prac- tically completed with the exception of two tanks that were being made on the upper side of the tannery. Tbe report was anoroved.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLES TOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLES TOWN.
LBY A CORRESPONDET]. FOOTBALL.

After receiving their quietus in the Lancashire Cup Competition at the hands of Stalybridge Rovers last week, Earlestown on Saturday were shuffled out of the English Cup Competition by St Helens Rens The game was a poor one from beginning to end and although the Rees won by two goals to nil their display did not warrant the victory. The Earlestown forwards played a dis— graceful game, and as a result bwholesale changes will be seen in to-morrow's front rank to face Southport central. A set of schoolboys could not have shaped worse than did the Earlestown quin- tette against the Rees, Leach, Settle and Tartan being the most conspicuous delinquents. These three players have been given a rest this week, Clare a local youth who has been playing with Burtonwood, taking Settle's place at outside-left whilst two men will displace Leach and Turton. Cotton will resume at left half-back in place of Limond who has not recovered from his injury. It will be interesting to see how these changes work.

Newton must be accounted unlucky in only get- ting one point out of their encounter with Middle- wich. The play during the first half was very even and the interval score about represented the game. During the second portion however, the Cheshire Club were only across the half-way line twice and on each of these occasions they took Jenkinson by surprise and registered a point. With a lead of three goals to one it looked odds on the visitors taking off the spoil, hut the homestera roused up and before the Close managed to draw level, after penning their opponents in their own quarters for over half an hour. During this bom- bardment Newton were awarded no less than three penalty kicks and they failed to net one of nem. One was taken by Lee who hit the bar, another by Butler who shot into the custodians hands and the third by Broster who followed Butler's example.
SAD DEATH OF MR. FRANK HOWARTH.

We regret to have to record this week the death of Mr Frank Howarth, second son of Mr George Howarth of Cross-lane,Earlestown at the earlyage of 27 years. For some considerable time he has been in employment away from home, and has only lately obtained a position at the Vulcan Foundry Newton. He has been apparently in good health, but one day last week after retiring to rest be was taken suddenly ill and Dr Mouncey was called in He diagnosed the case as appendicitis and recom- mended his removal to the Liverpool Infirmary, to undergo an operation. The operation was success- ful, and young Howarth up to Monday was pro- gressing satisfactorily. During the night however, mortification was set up,and despite every effort on the part of the Hospital staff, he passed away early on Tuesday morning. Ile was a promising young fellow'snd his sudden end has come as a severe blow to his father, brothers and sisters. SCHOOL PROSECUTION AT EARLEETOWN.—iIEATIC

LOCAL POOR RATES, on Saturday Messrs G L Davies and J Pritchard, sitting at the Runcorn Police Court, allowed poor rates tor Runcorn of is 2d in the pound, and for Norton township is 2d in the pouna. THE WYCLIFFE PREACHERS VISIT RUNCORN. During the week the celetorated Wycliffe preachers visited Runcorn. Each evening in the Market Hall Square services had been held before crowded gatherings. Happily there have been no serious disturbances. It is worthy of note that Superintendent Ennion made admirable provision in the event of any counter demonstration. VISIT OP REV. JAMES FLANAGA.N TO RUNCORN. On Wednesday next, theilsth just, this popular Evangelist and eloquent lecturer will preach at Greenway-road Chapel, in the afternoon and lecture in the evening. div.head: ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN MOTOR-CYCLIST.
div.p: ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN MOTOR-CYCLIST.

When proceeding from L3ominster to Runcorn on a motor cycle a few days ago Mr Carroll, jun., of Runcorn, run full tilt into a motorcar as he was going round a corner at Cotton, midway between Whitchurch and Wen. Toe bicycle was smashed, and its rider badly cut about the head and face, several of his teeth being knocked out. He was taken post-hasto in the motor car ro Shrewsbury, being unconscious all the way. His condition is described as serious. BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. At the weekly meeting of the above society Mr Alfred Dodd read a paper on Dr Beet's book "The Immortality of the soul." A brief epitome of the work was given, the essayist contending that Dr Beet's conclusions involved certain corollary infer- ences respecting the doom of the lost which the author could not logically deny. A discussion fol- lowed, in which Messrs W Millington, R H Posnett, W H Leathwood, and the chairman, the Rev Terry Coppin,took part. There was a very large attendance. MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMAN.—LAUNCEI OF A

div.head: STEAMER.
div.p: STEAMER.

A steamer of good proportions (50ft by 12 feet beam and 7 feet depth) was launched from the Lytham Shipbuilding Company's yard on Saturday afternoon for the use of the Mersey Mission. After a short service had been held by the Rev 13 Lambert, chaplain, the steamer was named the Good Cheer by Mrs Gibbon, and immediately took the water in grand style. There were also present Miss Cussans, Mr E Gibbon, Mr H L Payne, consulting enginneer, the Rev E M Savage, and the company's officials. It is expected that the new Good Cheer will be ready for useon the Mersey within a month. For the building fund about £3OO is still needed. SIIDDEN DEATH OF A WESTON GENTLEMAN. The death took place suddenly at the Birches, Weston, on Friday morning last week of Mr Joseph Banks, a member of a well-known Cheshire family. Since the death of his brother Thomas,some months ago, Mr Banks had been very depressed, and this appeared to have affected his general health. He was taken ill on Thursday night, and died before a doctor could be summoned. A post mortem was conducted by Dr McLennan on Saturday morning, and later in the day Mr E A White, deputy coroner held an inquiry. Evidence was given by Mr William Banks, eldest son, and Dr McLennan. Death was due to acute yellow atrophy of the liver. A verdict in accordance with the medical evidence was returned. The jury expressed their sympathy with the widow and family. P.O Wylie represented the police. THE BARSER CONCERT AT RUNCORN.

On Monday evening, Mr lom Barger, the popular comedian and vocalist, with his talent6d family, visited the Public Hall, Runcorn. From first to last the interest never flagged, the efforts of the artistes being applauded continuously by a large and enthusiastic audience. Mr Barger quite mystified his audience b 3 the rapidity with which he effected his different impersonations. In the first portion of the programme, the best item was unquestion- ably his famous " Sensation," which admirably portrayed a scene at Lime-street Station. In the second portion Miss Beta Barger and Messrs Nor- man Barger and Tom Barger, jun., vied with each other in supplying the audience with a series of items which were brimful of interest. A thoroughly high-class entertainment was brought to a conclu- sion by a ridiculously funny sketch by the Barger family. The entertainment was thoroughly enjoyed and the next visit of Mr Tom Barger will be eagerly awaited by Runcornians.
RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPoNDENT.]

The last meeting of the Rural Council throws no more light on the origin of the Thelwall nuisance. Mr Naylor has met tile Committee appointed to confer with him respecting the nuisance, but their findings are not very clear to the average .ndi- vidual. Pendirg further developments 1 the question rests in abeyance, and the nuisance goes on.

The Weaver authorities do not intend apparently to aid in the construction of any mortuaries, float- ing or otherwise, constructed to accommodate the bodies that may be recovered from the River Weaver They will, however, grant mooring places for such craft and think that in granting this favour their responsibility ends. As the Rural District Council do not feel justified in incurring any large( expendi- ture on this head the overseers of the respective parishes are to be approached on the subject. There can be no question that mortuaries of some des- Cription are absolutely necessary and the question is one of ways and meansiand who is to find them? I It is to be trusted that the difficulty can be sur- mounted.
Nonconformist Runcorn is slowly but surely awakening to the peril of the preaent Education

div.head: EDUCATION BILL.
div.p: THE EDUCATION BILL.
Free Church.t Protest at Runcorn.

On Monday evening a well-attended meeting "7311 held in the Halton-road Wesleyan Schoolroom, Runaorn, Mr J H Frith presiding, for the purpose of protesting against the Bducation Bill now before Parliament. The Chairman was supported by Ur F J Norman, the Rev Terry Oorpin, and Mr J bi Frith. .

The Chairman, explaining the purpose of the meeting, said he deeply regretted that they weie again called upon to fight a subject which he had thought closed, and closed for ever, but now he found that the old spirit that reigned years ago, before his time and in the time of his youth,the same domin- ant spirit, the same clerical influence, the same dogmatic teaching had arisen again. They were called upon io self- defenae toiput their foot down and fight against lt.lt was the same spirit that ruled in the time of Mary that reigned now i theCiourch ofllengland, The Church detested the very name on "dissenter," they hated the word '• nonconformity," and they were ready to put their shoulders side by side with the Roman Catholics to link arm with them and almost "go the whole hog" to drive the dissenters from their midst. Then he alluded in no unemphatic way to ritualistic practices in the Church. Now, as Non- conformists they stool on an equality with the Church as far as numbers were concerned, and they were determined that what their forefathers fought for and got should not be lost by them. He hoped and trusted that every Nonconformist in Runcorn would do his utmost to keep out the Ritualistic element, the Roman Catholic element, and everything that was derogatory, away from their Board Schools. they were asked to support Voluntary schools—schools wh re ignorance taught ignorance—where they tried to thrust down the throats of the yeung people that which was absurd and nonsensical, that" my little scholars" might become " my little Cnurehmen " imbued with the Ritualistic spirit. Were they going to stand that ? He hoped they were not going to support the Government, and he was glad to know that In the Northwleh division they did not help to put that Government into power, and were wise enough to return a good Liberal to Parliament—Sir join: Brunner. He hoped that every day would bring them closer to him and every- thing that was honourable and straightforward, and. that -they would raise their voices against this Education Bill brosight in by the Government. F d Norman then proposed :—" That this meeting of Runcorn citizens condemns the Government Education Bill. beeause it deprives men and women, who have hitherto elect ed or served upon School Boards of the constitutional rights they have hitherto enjoyed ; because it abolishes direct popular control of the schools for which the people are rated and taxed ; because it weakens the guarantee of efficiency. progress, and liberty in national education ; and because it proposes to levy local rates everywhere in support of sectarian dogmas' ecclesiastical teats for teachers, and clerical manage- ment. This meeting expresses its indignalon that the Government, without mandate or authority from the eleztorate, should propose to destroy' School Boards and to make sectarian schools a charge upon the. ratepayers. Finally the meeting calls upon the Prirw, Minister to withdraw the Bill or to dissolve Parliament." Mr Norman, in speaking to the resolutioa, dealt at cmsider able length with various phrases of the measure. At the outset he stated that he considered it a disgrace ihet at the dawn of the 20theentur7 they were called upon to propose such a resolution in this England of ours. That was the first of a series of meetings that they proposed to hold In Runcorn but the first question was how in the world this had all been brought about. It would seem that whilst my lord of Devon- shire had been waiting for a breeze. whilst Mr Balfour had been up in the clouds, and boasting that he never read the newspapers, whilst their friend Chamberlain had been busy in the other department and the country had been spending money and shedding its beet blood to give constitutional government and a sound educational system to South Africa the clerical party had been grinding their own axe. It seemed to him that they had bagged the Ministry and that there was a barefaced attempt to prostitute an Imperial majorityßor purely sectarian ends: The word "clericalism ' formed the whole crux of the question He dsfiued " clericalism "as the effect of any religious organization seeking to take hold of the public good to utilise it for purely sectarian purposes. Quoting the historian Green, himself a Church of England minister, when writing to his contemporary historian Freeman on the subject, he read "What hinders education and accounts for its want among the people? Whet hinders education but our attempt to make It sectarian and not national? " The question of control as set forth in the Bill was nothing short of ridiculous. In the measure the clerical party had staked their all,but if they once got into power, ant the young children into their hands: they would be able to rehabilitate themselves and work back to power. Even the Conservative party were not in Word on the measure, and some 100 members were opposed to it, but whether they would have courage to actively oppose it was another matter. Proceeding, he showed that by the system of selecting the new single authority was by co-optation first of all of a general committee by the County Council, and this committee to co-opt the local committee, upon which they were allowed two representatives. That was inade- quatereand absurd, and meant nothing short of disen- franchisement. Working with a hopeless majority of this kind they could not hope to oppolnt masters other than Churehmen,and if they were successful in getting an, assistant in, and the master went away or died, would they putting themselves in the earns position, blame that assist- ant, poorly paid and perhaps with a family to keep, and seeing the chance of his life before him, If he turned Church- man. He did not regret the Bill because it had caused people to read the question. If it came to fighting for this Bid he had some very concrete cases to quote from Runcorn of influence brought to bear upon the young and orthe work of , proselytization. In conclusion he briefl r touched upon the ' question of buildings, and promised that he would refer to this point again. Finally he said he hoped that they would say emphatically to the Government that they must have a proper and nobler system worthy of a free people. Mr J 111 Frith seconded briefly. Alluding to the voluntary school buillingsliee said their value was variously said to be 20 to 40 millions sterling, hut they found that they could re- place the Voluntary schools for £23,000,000, and be would leave them to judge whether the Church schools In Runcorn were not worse than the Board schools. In an article in the " Parish Magazine," Canon Wood asked was it fair to rob the Church of their buildings? He would ask in turn. Who said anything about robbing them? They were ready to buy or rent them. He thought Canon Wood was fond of putting up a skittle to knock it down again, for throughout his letter he had put up skittles only to knock them down again. The Chairman put the resolution, which was carried an animously. _ - _ _ _

div.head: Meeting at the Ashridge-street Mission.
div.p: Meeting at the Ashridge-street Mission.

At the Ashridge-street Mission the second of the series o meetings protesting against the Education Bill was held on Tuesday erening.—Rev Sidney Morris occupied the chair, and he was supported by Messrs R H Posnett, W Handley, A It Norman, and others. The Chairman. in the course of a vigorous speech, said if the Bill became law it would deprive them of civil and religious liberty. It was virtually a confession that the Church of England had failed to carry on their schools in spite of the aid of rates, ttc. The Government had been elected on one issue, and it was a mean advantage to take of the very people who had put them in They should fight against the Bill heart and soul. Dr Robertson Nicholl advocated passive resistance to the supporting of those schools for the propagation of dogmas that they hated. As they did not believe in them they would not, must not, and dare not support them. What then were they to do ? It was their duty to °Won to pay their rates. He for one had resolved that he would not pay a rate for the support of schools that taught what was objectionable to his I conscience. He hoped they would stand firm shoulder to , shoulder and the fight would be won. (Applause). Mr Handley in proposing the usual resolution against the Bill, said that the fight was not of their seeking. The Government were seeking to alter the whole of their educa- tional system from top to bottom. The two points at issue were popular control and religious tests for teachers It would 'e never come to a non-payment of rate Already the Anglicans were talking of compromise Bat it was for them (the ratepayers) to dictate the terms. The time for compromise from the opposite party had gone. (Applause). The speaker then dealt with the work of the Board in Runcorn and Cheshire and criticised advisely the claim that voluntary schools belonged to particular sects. Mr Posnett seconded. He field they ought to look at the question from the standpoint ol a citizen. The end to be secured was justice to children. They asked for the citizens right that they who pay should manage. If ever thd show had been given away—if ever a Pope had proved his infalli- bility a show—it was when Mr Joseph Chamberlain called a conference with the Liberal unionists at Birmingham. They in Runcorn would not be the greatest sufferers. There were good villages which contained schools where the Vicar was absolute. Mr Posnett proceeded to criticise at length he Vicar's letter in the Parish Magazine and concluded by 'Wring all to stand firm. The resolution was passed aninimously by Mr A R Norman supporting.

On Wedneaday and Thursday evenings similar protest meetings to the above were held In the Primitive and Bruns- Wick schoolrooms. On both occasions resolutions protesting against the Education Bill were unanimously passed.

Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds— Warrington District. The quarterly meeting of this district was held on Saturday at the Rose Bud Lodge, St. James Schoolroom, Latchford. Bro Joseph Adams the D Pro :C S apologised for the absence of the district chief, Bro Joseph Williams, who he regretted to state was suffering from a serious complaint. There were present Trustees Bros Eckersley and Hall, District Treasurer Bro James Parr, and District Secretary Bro P Edgar and the delegates from the various lodges belonging to such district. Thera were also several visiting brethren present. The quarterly accounts were read, and found to be of a satisfactory character, and on the auditors reporting that the same had been found correct, the accounts were unanimously passed A pleasing feature of the meeting was the present- ation to Bro John Haley of a handsome sideboard cabinet in recognition of his past services as Pro C Shepherd of the district for the year 1901-2. The presentation was made by tiro Thos Miller, who spoke in glowing terms of the very valuable ser- vices rendered by Bro. Haley, and the great help he had been in pushing forward the claims and bene- fits lof Shepherdry. He trusted that he would appreciate the present, and hoped that he and his wife and!family would:have their lives prolonge for many years to come to enjoy the same. Bro Millers remarks were warmly and earnestly endorsed by Bro T S Massey, Lawrence Weir, James Parr, William Hall, Joseph Adams and others. Bro Haley thanked the Brettren for their kind words, and present.

Annual Meeting.

The annual meeting of the subscribers to the committee of the Runcorn District Nurse Fund was held in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall on Monday afternoon, The Vicar (the Rev Canon Maitland Wo)d) presided, and there were also present Mrs RlHick, Mrs Abel. Miss Andrews, Mrs Handley, Mrs Barker, Mrs Imlson, Mrs Wood (hen secretary), Mr F Lake (bon treasurer), the Rev if B Frit and Mr Priestley.

THE REPORT. Tke Committee's report was as follows":—Your committee thankfully put on record the completion of the thirteenth year of the wark of the nurse fund. Your committee have been able. Curing the year, to send 13 children to West Kirby Conva:e.cent Home, and ten adults to Wooltou Con- valescent Home.from the mast kindly provided by Miss Plerpolnt and her friends and they consider that it would be difficult to exaggerate the advantages of having this fund at disposal. The numiaer of persous visited by the nurses during the year was 241, viz. :—Patients receiving regular visite, 127, viz e—Medical, 57, received. 799 Visits ; surgical, 43, received 591 ; typhoid 30 received, 660. Patients receiving occasional visite 114 ; number of visits, 799 ; total number of visits, 2,849. Of the 127 oases visited during the year 70 are convalesodnt. 34 have died. 3 have gone to hospitaft. 4 have been put on tde Occasional Visits Lists and 17 are still on the hooks. The act sat number of visits is not quite so large as last year. but it should be noted that the Typhoid Cases arose from 11 to 33, ant the visits to Ty- phoid asses from 259 to 663. The committee are constituted as follows, and retire in rotation in the following order 1-1939. Mesdames Abel, MacLennan, Maieland Wood ; 1933, Mrs Barker, Miss Andrews ; 19 4. Mesdames Walter T•mnains, William Kay, Killick ; 19.15. Mesdames Imison, T Handley, B.ker. A rule passed at the annual meeting in 1903, which should have appeared in the report for 1901, was omitted, it is presumed by inadvertence, and now appears for the first time. The report was adopted •

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday. James Binom- ial& 13. Selby-street, Warrington was charged with having been drunk and disorderly In Gartwright-street on Saturday might, and with having committed aggravated assaults noon his mother and wits—P.o Sennett maid that at 10.15 ea Saturday night he saw the prisoner in the midst of a large crowd of people in 'Cartwright- street. shouting and making use of bed language.— Prisoner's mother. who is 66 years 'of age, stated that her son and his wife had been residing with her for a llienth. On Saturday afternoon prisoner canto horns drunk and began quarrelling with his wife. Prisoner's father went between them and was struck by the prisoner. Mee daughter- in-law ran oat of the house as prisoner was going to strike her, and when witness west to Call her back the prisoner threw a dolly-peg at her. This struok her on the arm and inflicted a nasty wound which had to be stitched at the Infirmary. Prisoner had no provocation. Oa Sunday h. was again quarrelling with his wife. and Ist trying to prevent his violenoe witness received a blow on the arm which caused diseelenration. Prisoner,however,whilst in the back kitchea struck his wife on the head with his fist, and knocked her down.—Blizabeth Gertrude Bloomfield, prisoner's wife, gave Corroborative evidence, She said prisoner kicked her in the ribs whilst she was ea the ground, and she was obliged to ran out of the hesse as she was in danger of her life many times If the magistrates convicted him she would spray for a separation erder.—Prisoner said he was drank and did net know what he was doing.—The Bench sent him to gaol for three months.

Mary Warburton. of Nicholson-street, appeared in the dock at the -Warrington Police Court on Wednesday charged With stealing by means of a trick on September 4th. El Os 6d, the naceieys of Mary Ann Chantler, her next doer neighbour.— She pleaded guilty. -The Chief Constable said the theft had been committed under peculiar and unusual ciroumstances. Mrs Chantler was a married woman, and was the wife of John Bens" Chestier, a platelayer who resided at 33, Nicholson- street. She was a member of the Co operative Stores, lad en September 3rd brought her book home. In the book was registered a certain amount of money, to her credit from deposits or dividend. Ti.. amount due to prosetutrix was RI OS 63. When she zet home the prisoner came into the house. After a time conversation turned upon the C.- operative Stores, and the drisoner asked the proseentrix if her book was all right. She said " Yes.' and showed it to her. Sense time afterwards the prosecutris fell ill, and the prisoner took the opportunity of coming into the house several times and doing various slices. This week Mr Chantler found that his usual holidays were due, and the book was hunted up for the perpose isf providing the where- withal for him to take a perhaps much needed vacation. The book. however, was net forthconsing, and inquiries were male at the Co-operative Stores. when it was found that the money had been drawn int on the 4th of September. by someone signing herself' Moiden," who produced a doou- anent as Mrs Chentler's written authority to withdraw the money. The doenment read :—" Dear sir please allow bearer to have the amount of 21 Os 6.1 and oblige Mrs Chantler." There was a rule of the Co-operative Seeiety which said that money would be paid to members only or on their written authority. Ti.. employes of the society having what purnerted to be the prosecutries written signature,pald oat to the woman Mrs Clbantler's money. The offence amounted to forgery, of course, but so that it might be Moult with by the magistrates he had brought up the ease as •Ild of larceny. Probably the woman did not know the normality of the offence. The society's cash beak was signed with the name of B Holden. That was %nether serious feature of the case as the prisoner not only forged Mn Shantler's name but that of a yenng -woman who lived In the neighbourhood, a perfectly innocent woman who had abs,,l,t,oy no knowledge of either the prose- nutrix or prisoner, sad wh4 naterally fell under the

Immediate suspicioa of the police. Ile thought Lira was a very bad feature, as the prisoner not only robbed one WOlllan but tried to throw suspicion ea the blameless character et another. The matter having been reported to the police, Superintendent Monaghan and 'Detective Barlow visited the prisoner's house. She at first denied all Icnswledge of ths oßence. but subsequently admitted it mid said she had • not I done any good since.' Ile had been iaformed that she was a I woman of intemperate habits, and probably took the money for drink. —The Chairman said the class was • rery serious one. If the Chief Constable had not altered the °barge the prisoner would have to go for trial at the Qaarter Sassiest. and she would probably hays been severely dealt with there. As this was her Int offence the Beach wield give her the option of paying a due of 4s and costs, or in default one month's imprisonment. —Tao Chief Ceneable remarked that he had Seen people get ten years' penal servitude for a less erieus offense.

Railway Smash at Bank Quay Station: The low level railway station at sank Quay was the scene of a railway smash on Saturday morning. An empty passenger train was being shunted front the Arpley Station into the bay at Bank Quay and before the driver could bring it to a standstill it dashed with Rreat forc9 into a guard's van which was standing near the stop block. The force of the impact dislodged the step-block and damaged a small portion of the platform. Several of the carriages in the centre of the train viers wrecked, two of them leaving the metals. Fortnnately neither the driver nor the stoker sustained any injury. The train was due te leave Bank Quay Station fer Londou-roafl at &30 a.m., :but it was munif later before coaches could be obtained to replace those which had been damagel.

div.head: Warrington Field Club.
div.p: Warrington Field Club.

There was a good attendance at the Museum Lecture room at the opening meeting of the winter 1 session, whoa the eutomologists displayed some of ' the results of their simmer work. The new Pro- eideat (Mr F %rentersley), and Messrs W Mountield, Collins, Howarth, Wright, and Burton, exhibited moths, dragonfliss, and beetles, all remarkable in some way, either for beauty of form or colour, rarity or special variations, and for the most part captured in Lancashire or Cheshire. Captain I Fairelongh showed several boxes of insects, I the result of work done during his leisure hours whilst serving with the Warrington attachment in the recent Beer war. They wets much admired,and his description.? the conditions under which they had been taken, preserved, and brought to England was listened to with interest and keen attention, by an audience meat of whom were competent to realise the difficulties Captain Fairclongis had had to contend with, and could, therefore, appreciete his energy and zeal. Each of the local exhibitors spoke upon his season's work, and a diseussion followed in which Mr Charles White, Mr Greening, and Mr Madoloy joined. The influence of food upon the colour of insects had I been alluded to, and Mr Greening, who had boon making prolonged observations upon thia subject, j leaned to the opinion that there is little if any colt- 1 suction between them. He promised to lay the re- sults of his researches before the club at a future date. Several gifts were made to the Museum out of tlae series exhibited. The enrichment of the eollections in the Municipal Museum is one of the specific objects of the Field Club, and the mere money value of the 'donations made by its members aggregates hundreds of pounds. Not less import- ant is the goad feeling which has always been maintained in this very democratic scientific society where professional business and working men meet on equal and friendly terms, and where anyone in- terested in natural history is welcome. Students desirous of joining the club may obtain informa- tion about it at the Musetna, or from the hos see - rotary, Councillor A J Jolley.

div.p: WARRINGTON CORPORATION

inspection of the Wilderspool Route.

Lieutenant-Colonel von Dollop, an inspector o t,he Beard of Trade, visited Warrington on Friday is.r the purpose of inspecting the Wilderspool sec- tion of the tramways prior to their us o by the The Inspector was met at the Town Hall by the Ceairman of the Tramways Committee (Alderman Henry Roberts), Alderman Hutchinson, „Councillors John Evans, A Bennett, S Davies, D S liancan, J Smethurst, John Sampson, T B Malkin, tlajor Cardew (consulting engineer), Mr J Lyon IVhittle (town clerk), Mr T Longdirt (borough sur- leYor). Mr J Fairhurst (borough treasurer), Mr W H 'irisasdale (tramways manager), Mr F V L Mathias sesistant), and Mr Evvart (contractor). Two cars were brought into use and a start was made from the general post office in Sankey-street Shortly after 10 30 a in. On reaching the Waders- pool level railway crossing, a thorough inspection Was made by the inspector of the arrangements 'Which had been made for obviating accidents there. l'ere the party was joined by Mr Andrews and Mr LYtich and the stationmaster at Warrington (repre- senting the London and North-Western Company) cud Air Heath (general post office.) .xeellent arrangements have been made at the railway crossing for expeditiously opening and elssing the gates, and for preventing the cars from rennin into the gates when closed. The closing the gates automatically causes the overhead table which conveys the current to become " dead " ler a certain distance on both sides of the gates. 71113 provision prevents any car from reaching ,t gates even if the brakes on the vehicle Si! to ac,. In order to thoroughly test u :s arrangement the Inspector caused the gates 'Jo 'le closed and asked for the cars to °a allowed to run towards them without the appli- cation of the brake. This was done and it was ,110ticed that the car came to a standstill within a yards after reaching the " dead " section of the overhead wire, and stopped at least ten yards from the gates. These precautionary measures Should re--assure the most timorous of the ,Isfety of the tramway system. The inspector put Ole apparatus to a severe test yesterday and ex- Pressed himself as satisfied with it. His report will °a received in the course of a few days.

div.p: First Division.

WARRINGTObf WIN AT BATLBY.' A smart performance was accomplished by Warrington en Saturday when they visited Mount Pleasant, Batley, and defeated the "gallant youths " on their own ground. For the first' time since his injury last February, Isherwood turned eat and captained the Warringten team, which was at praetieally full strength. Batley were also well represen- ted, giving a trial at half to Hodgson, late of Bradford. The weather WAS again excellent, if cold, and there was a good crowd of spectators. Mr Smith, the referee, was a bit late, and the teams turned out ten minutes after the advertised time. They were composed as follows : Batley Fozzard, full back ; Davies. Fitzgerald, Roebuck. and Kershaw, three-quarters ; Oakland and Hodgson, half- backs ; Spurr, Moseley, Wolstenholme, Robinson, Judge, Munns,lPhilllps and Farrar. forwards. Warrington: Knight, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dicken- son and Harris, three-quarters ; Burgess and Hooks:shall, half backs ; Boardman, Taylor, Morrison, lEdmendeon , Fors- ter. 3 Swift. IN Swift, and Roberts, forwards. Warrington lost the toss and 3 Swift started against a stiff breeze, bat with the slope in his favour. Warrington get possession from the first pack, Burgess passing badly be Heekenhall, wise was collared. Then Warrington got away again, Burgess, Hookenhall, Isherwood and Fish passing finely. The latter sprinted down to the corner and then centred, Forster fielding and running over near the posts where he lost the ball and there was no try. It was a lucky escape for Haley. The referee awarded numerous penalties for "feet-up " and from one of these near touch Fish placed a capital goal. This roused "the gallant youths" and they rushed to the Warrington quarter where Davies get a penalty kick and hit the upright with a good shot. Dickenson replied with a mighty punt in touch in the Batley half. Then a mull by Knight gave the hemesters another footing in the Warrington half and Davies tried again for goal but was wide of the mark. Warrington attaeked again, Diakea- son taking a dying pass from the pack and almost running through. • moment later he sprinted half the length of the field and passed forward to Burgess. Werrington were having all the play and it was only the ears tackling of Batley whish kept their speedy oppoaents out. Fish had another penalty shot but did no better than Davies. Batley attacked again as the result of exehange kicking. and Hodgson hesitated when he had a grand open- ing, which at once closed up. Batley were very troublesome for a few minutes, and Phillips wee pulled down on the line by Harris. Warrington carried the scrimmage and went to the other end, where there was a fierce battle on the home line, Burgess, Hockenhall and Herds ban all but over. The homesters eventually clearing by short stages along the touch line. Later Forster picked up in the loose and threw to Isherwood who gave Fish a pass which the latter miesed, with a good opening before him. Half-time, Warrington, 1 goal ; Batley, nil, The second half was practically a repetien of the first. Warriegton attacking the major portion of the time but fall- ing to get through by the nearest of " shaves." Dickensea did some huge pointing with the wind. and Batley could make no headway a% all, their efforts to find touch being uncommonly feeble. Exciting play followed fine follow-up and tackle of Fozzard by Harris. Fitzgerald and Davies changed the venom with pretty passing and re- passing, which finally went: forward. Isherwood sprinted back to the home quarter and then kicked, Fish and Davies having a race for the tall which the latter &insured under the posts and punted into safe quarters. Than Hookenhall broke clean away from the pack and ran nearly to the line, where he was held. • pass from hien would have got Warrington a oertain try but he wont too far. Batley got down to the Warrington half again,and Oakland punted across for Davies bat Harris sent in touoti. A moment later the trick was tried again, and the speedy Welshman got to the ball as soon as Harris. The latter made sure of the man and referee Smith awarded a penalty amid great excitement. Davies jost.tipped the ball and dashed over the tine.butiwas brought back and the homesters were ordered to scrimmage. "Time" arrived the next minute and Warrington had won a fine game by 2 points to nil. RUNCORN v. BRIGHOUSE RANGERS. There was a very poor attendance at Irviell-lane en Saturday to witness the performance of the above teams. Both sides were representative Runcorn were unfortunete In losing the toss, and commenced operations against breeze and sun. After preliminary skirmishes play settled down at midfield, where some un nteresting play was witnessed. Bventnally the home forwards broke away in finestyle.Bavllle saving nicely. • splendid bit of combination aided by a nut run of Warder's gained considerable ground, but the defence war more than equal to the attaolc. A dangerous rush af the visitors saw the Runcorn line in danger buoy and Houghton showing conspicuously in finding touch. For some time scrambling play followed, the visitors being penalized repeatedly. Play oontinthed open anal exciting but neither side could gain any material advantage A forward move- ment started by Jolley nearly ended disastrously for Brighouse. Moran securing and dropping the leather in the good mouth among a pack the bail being touched down. A rush forward by the visitors tools the leather to the Runcorn end, where from a 'grumbling bit of play Sutcliffe soared at the corner. Seville failing to convert. After this reverse the Linnetts tried hard to make an impression a Sae effort by Jolley and Richardson deserving success. The visitors still kept the upper hand Jolley nulling badly in his own lines. A moment later Jolley was foully charged by Smith and was laid out for some time. Smith was sent off the field. Half- time :—Brighouse one try, Runeorn nil. On the restart Runcorn forced the game at a rapid rate. Jolley found touch neatly and placed his side on the offensive. Shortly after Jones gathered and handed to Houghton who made a brilliant run to the visitors lines where he was collared in the nick of time. Scrimmage after scrimmage was made on the line but with no roeult, the leather eventu- ally being worked out of danger. Richardson in turn having to touch down. Jolley cleared, Runcorn making a desperate effort to pierce the defense. Brighouse attached strongly in turn, scrimmaging on the home lines, giving Runcorn an anxious five minutes. Jolley cleared again, Warder trying to get away. From a neat kick by the same player Moran had a splendid chance and made the most of it but was grassed at the corner. Some exciting play followed but Run- corn could not get along at all, the Rangers breaking up every combination. Runcorn were not to be denied, however, and after a p articularly fierce Onslaught Butterworth steered through his opponents and scored, Farmer falling. Both sides got to work in grim earnest after this and a few minute. I later Moran scored after the leather had been handled by all home backs, the goal kick failing. Another burst by the home team saw the visitors lines in danger and Moran again having a chance to slip in but parting with the ball. Jones made a fine run initiating a movement which led to Warder ; scoring. Jolley failed at goal. A little later Miller was sent ' off the field for striking Jones in the face while he Was on the ground. orambling play followed to tho Close. Final : Runcorn, three tries ; Brighouse one try. LEIGH Y. WIDNES. At Leigh, before 4,003 spectators. Widnes kicked off against a rather strong breeze. and play was even for seine time until Peacock stole a Leigh pass. and with a clear open- ing seemed to have a good chance of scoring, bat he was overhauled and pulled down. The Leigh backs started pass- ing, and first Ganley and then Barr were pulled down dangerously near the line. Another pass was intercepted by Taylor, but again the lack of speed proved fatal, Ganloy catching him easily. For the remainder of this half play was mostly dull, and at the interval there was me score, Leigh now had the strong wind against them, but their forwards repeatedly gained possession in the scrimmages, with the result that Leigh attacked hotly. Hinson, Ganley, Bennett. and Molyneux all tried ,to break threugh in turn. but were checked, and then Molyneux with grand judgment punted across to Ganley, who took the ball on the run and registered a try.no goal resulting. Leigh again attacked.and Barr missed a certain try by mulling Bennett's pass near the line. The game favoured Leigh to the end. Result : Leigh 1 try, Widnes nil. div.head: LANCASHIRE RUGBY COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE RUGBY COMBINATION.
A VICTORY FOR WARRINGTON "A."

Virarrirgtou "IA" entertained St Helens " A" at Wilders- pool on Saturday, and retired victors by eleven points to nil. There was a fair attendance of spectators. St Helens kieked off against the wind, and the start was a sensational one, for Webb had his kiek charged down, and a bt Helens forward was pulled up only a foot from the line, For a time the visitors pressed hard. but good forward play by Warrington gradually worked the ball up the field, and Eden got over, but the point was disallowed. Warrington still pressed, and a good round of passing ended in Duckworth sooring,Knight kieking a goal. Shortly afterwards Webb scored a second try, and a few minutes later Brooks ran over somewhat easily. The goal kicks were abortive. Half-time :—War- rington 1 goal 3 tries. St Helens nil. Fairhurst restarted, and St Helens had the best of the play for the first ten minutes. Maguire having hard lines in not scoring. War- rington were without Webb during the greater part of the second half, owing to that player sustaining an injury to the leg. Play was very uninteresting. neither side scoring. Flnal.—Warrington " A" 11 points, St Helens ail.

div.head: Wycliffe Young People's Society.
div.p: Wycliffe Young People's Society.

This society commenced the 1902-3 session on Monday evening under auspicious circumstances. The new assembly hall in the Memorial Building was filled with a gathering of young folks who spent a most enjoyable social evening. A pro- gramme of songs, glees, &c., occupied the first portion of the proceedings. The Pastor (Rev John Yonge) occupied the chair and briefly sketched the society's programme for this year. He ex- pressed an earnest hope that the society :would continue its useful career with even greater success than in the past, especially as they now had that beautiful room at their disposal. Solos were effici- ently sung by Mrs Arthur Booth, Miss B Smith and Mr Arthur Griffiths. Mrs Booth and Mr Griffiths were also heard together in a duet. A glee party under the direction of Mr Gauld sang several glees in a highly creditable manner. Mr Tom Wallington presided at the piano. Miss Beswick recited in her usually acceptable manner. Refreshments which had been kindly supplied by Mr and Mrs John Atkinson were handed ,round during an interval and the remainder of the evening was pleasantly whiled away in games.
