div.p: NOTES ON (JAMES AND ATHLETICS, --- Rugby Footba:l. {Bv Ovalist.l No league success could probably have gratified the Warrington players and supporters more than the vic- tory at Batley on Saturday. There is almost as much rivalry between the clubs as there is between the South West Lancashire teams, due entirely to the fact that Warrington and Batley have had a few tussles in the concluding stages of the Northern Union Cup Competi- tion, when, unfortunately, the "gallant youths " always came off best. Last season each side won at home, but the odds are now very much in favour of Warrington getting the best of the bargain this season, seeing that Batley have yet to visit Wilderspool.

Form suggested that Warrington should win on Saturday, but then the Batley men have an unpleasant habit of upsetting predictions based on so illusory a thing as" form." For once, however, it was reliable, though the margin of Warrington was so exceedingly narrow—a solitary goal to nil—that, on the face of things, it would seem there was an element of luck in the victory. Such was not the case, though, Warring- ton's victory being the outcome of such superior play as kept Batley on the defensive during three parts of the game.

I am very glad that Isherwood's return to the captaincy was signalised by such a handsome victoiy. How much difference he makes in the team was very apparent on Saturday. The whole of the backs moved al ng to the attack in a fashion which was quite'ex- hilaratin.g, and which has been foreign to them for some time " Dan " himself was as good as ever, his play being full of characteristic dash and self-confi- dence. I hope he is safe for the rest of the season, now the ice has been broken, and that we shall hear Lie more of knee troubles.

The match started some ten minutes late owing to the non-arrival at 3.30 of Mr J Smith, who—like somel other great men—cuts matters pretty fine in the way of keeping appointments. He is such a smart referee, however, that one can forgive his tardy arrival as long as he comes at all. At one time it looked as if the Warrington team wa-, also going to he late, for some nameless idiot at Ashton-under-Lyne uncoupled our -saloon from the Hudders2eld:express,which consequent- ly left us lamenting in the station, with sad thoughts of the good lunch spoiling at the " George." There were some expressions of opinion from players who had breakfasted about 6 a in which were the reverse of polite a, d would have done the individual who un- coupled the saloon a world of good could he have only heard them. Things eventuated better than litely, however, and a slow train landed us in Huddersfiold at 1.30, threequarters of an hour late. The lunch was not spoiled and there was just time to do it full justice and catch a convenient train to Batley, which was reached at 3 o'clock.

At Batley they get about the same size of crowd as is usually seen at Widnes and Runcorn, and with the people of the district the Warrington match is a popu- lar one. There would bi about 2000 spectators on Saturday and no doubt 199 of them expected to see Warrington comfortably quashed, as in the pasc In this respect they we..e disappointed, but they did not let their chagrin overcome their fairness,and the rounds of applause in recognition of Warrington's good play were frequent.

From the commencement the visitors showed their superiority both forward and back in unmistakable fashion. The front rank men kept up their previous good form and it was refreshing to see them taking the ball time after time from the home scrummagers. Batley were scarcely as strong here as they used to be, but they nevertheless possessed a pack which looked strong enough to hold Warrington up. Burgess and Hocken- hall made good use of the frequent opportunities vouch- safed them, and the three-quarter line was continually on the move—and moving in a fashion which showed how important Isherwood is as the connecting link with Fish. The latter was twice nearly over, and wh' n he kicked across for Forster to run in, the few Warring- tonians present were joyful. The joy was premature, for the referee disallowed the point, and he was in a good position to see all that occurred. Two minutes later Fish landed a penalty goal with a fine kick from near touch, and this proved to be the winning point The penalty was for " feet up," which Mr. Smith rigorously put down, and before half-time he had con- vinced the forwards that it was unnecessary to hook for the ball before it was in the scrummage. Warrington were penaized as often as Batley, and Davies had two attempts at making the score level, but failed, though his first shot went so near as to hit the upright.

The second half was just as much in favour of War- rington as the first,Batley being seldom in the Warring- ton quarter. It was really remarkable show the Warrington backs were kept out, considering the num- ber of times they ran down with the ball and seemed certain to score. " Wattie " Davies once robbed Fish of a try under the posts, a race between the two ending in favour of the Batley man by the thickness of his jersey. The two men were running from opposite sides, Isherwood having kicked into the goal mouth. The combination of the Warrington backs was really excellent, and in my opinion they have not run and passed so well since the time they were running through the Cup Competition last season but one. Batley after one or two efforts which were promptly nipped in the bud by the Warrington centres, gave the pa ssing game up and went in for wheeling the scrummages, and short dashes. Davies, in consequence, was neglected, which was a good thing for Warrington as he is unquestion- ably the most dangerous three-quarter whom they have to face. Teams which have to watch both Davies and Fish twice a season are unfortunate.

The game was exceedingly well-contested, the score indicating how resolute was the Batley defence There was no " dirty " play either, and Mr Smith is to be given much of the credit for this. Last year's match was more or less a fight, and the contrast on Saturday was very pleasing. The best man on the Warrington side was Dickenson who played a great game both on attack and defence. His punting alone kept Batley defending, while in running, passing, and tackling he was at his best. In fact the whole of the backs were tip top,with the exception of Knight who was unsteady at times. The halves were very "nippy " and got away cleverly. Each had his faults,however. Burgess has a tendency to pass recklessly and Ilockenhall runs too far with the ball, often getting his own and the opposing centres hopelessly mixed. A little more judgment in passing at the right moment is required from both. Davies was the one " star "of the Batley team and he was unlucky in failing to score, though he was not alone in this respect The other " gallant youths " tackled well and worked hard, but were obviously short of skill and speed.

On Monday I went to Widnes to see the trial game between Probables and Possibles, and was rewarded for my pains with as fine a display of scientific football as I have seen for years. There was an absence of great excitement, of course, but one a-as sorry when the end came, the play was so bright and interesting. Then again, Fish, Dickenson and Boardman assisted the Probables, while Harris operated on the left wing of the Possibles. All four played in a style which did the Warrington Club credit. Dickenson, indeed, was the best threequarter on the field, even ".Bob ."Wilson being inferior to the dashing young Wamngtoman,who fairly came out of his shell when " fed " by two such half-back artistes as the Jameses. How much depends on the halves was amply demonstrated by the improve- ment as a centre in Dickenson. He not only scored two grand tries, but gave Evans the ball on a third occasion when he had reached the line, while Fish also scored one of his two tries irom Dickenson's pass. I wish our halves had the genius of these two Welshmen The threequarters would get tries galore !

It is most unfortunate for rickenson that there is so good a centre as R Valentine available for the County, otherwise he would be certain of the place. As it is he is first reserve. while Harris is chosen as reserve right wing. an honour he earned by sterling play at Widnes. Fish and Boardman are among the elect, and both won their caps in the trial game, which was rather remarkable for the fact that the Broughton wing pair failed to score. On the rossibles side Lomas was the hero, scoring all the points and doing the bulk of the work ire tip-top fashion. He is quite the best individual half•back en the Northern League. Warrington will need to watch him carefully to-day when Salt d are visited. or

MUNICIPAL TRADING.
The Financial Position of the Corporation. _ Mr. Dodds Writes for Information. Interesting Statement by Alderman Shaw Green.

At the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening spme interesting statistics were given by Alderman Shaw Green kchairman of the Finance and Eitate Committee) relative to the cost of buildings recently erected in the town and also as to the indebted- ness of Oa Borough. Ttia statement was made in answer to the following Ltter which bld been addressed b the Town Clerk by Mir James Doctig. _ _

" Dear Mr Town Clerk,—May I ask you to be so kind as to give me the following information, namely, the total expenditure to date on the new Felice Courts, dit:o on the Technical Schools, ditto on ths Hill Warren reservoir, ditto on the new pipe male Winwick Delph-lane pumping 6tatina and ncw wells contract, ditto on the Winwick new storage reservoir, also the present total indehtedciPs of the county borough upon loans, apart from the lyink overdraft (if any), and the amount of the present bank over- draft (if any) ? Of course approximate figures would serve ; if you have not these at hand, peroaps you will kindly bring my request before the Finance Committee, which I observe is to rnPet on Monday next, the 6th inst.—Th4nlcing you in anticipation I _ _

_ am, yours faithfully.—JAMES DODDS. Alderman SHAW GREEN said the Town Clerk very properly brought this letter before the Finance and Estate Committee, who felt that it was only right that a courteous and full reply should be given to it. (Hear, hear.) The committee also thought that the inform- ation, which was interestuarz and valuable, should at the earliest moment be placed before the Council generally. I hope the Council will approve of the sugeestion and will give me a few minutes while I answer each of the questions separately, (Hear, hear.)
THE NEW POLICE COURT.

1 The eetimated Pxpenditure on these buildings when the matter was before the Counott was £25000. The con- tracts entered into, and other ,;urna which have not been specially contracted for, bring the amount to £24,966, but in addition to these contractg we have spent other moneys, including the purchase of the land and so forth and up to the present there has been expended £26,823 03 1.1.1.

div.head: TECNICAL SCHOOL.
div.p: TECNICAL SCHOOL.

The estimate for these schools was £15,000. The com- mittee took over that tract of land lying between Palmyra-lquare and Mweurr-street—a very valuable and important plot. We shall not use the whole of it even when the entire set of buildings is finished ; so that althongh I am giving &wens which represent the total value of the land, there will be some portion to be treated as aa asset when the buildinzs are complete. £15,000 was the estimate for that portion of the work that wil very shortly be ready tor opening. The build- logs erected, and the land make a total reaper's° of £19,148 2s 7d the actual amount of payments made being £15,593 64 4d.

WATER WORKS EXTENSIONS. Ti Warrenfreservoir, new pipe main, Delph-lane pumping station, Winwick, new storage reservoir ; these I are four items, but I cannot give you the estimated expenditure. It has been point,s3 out to the Committee that it would be manifestly unfair in any contract now ,in hand to let any one know what the expected or the estimated cost would be ; but the contracts which have been entered into, I will give. On the Nill Warren reservoir the cantracts are £6,748, the payments on that account being £6,615. New pipe main from Winwick to Hill Waven Tne contracts are £7,137, amount paid £7,005 18s 7d. The Delph-lane pumping station, wells, l nd, and so forth,contracts, £32,671 108 ; actual expenditure for payments to date £1.7,487. Tee new storage reservoir at Win wick : The contract for that was £20,456 18s 73, actual nrney paid £16,956. I said just now that it would not be fair to give the amoant the Committee anticipate] by the estimates given to them of the cost of these works, but I will venture to say that the Committee feel that they can congratulate themselves that on the contracts that have been entered into practically in every case they are within the esti- mated expenditure. (Hear, hear).
THE BOROUGH DEBT AND THE RANK OVERDRAFT.

The debt of the borough apart from the bank over- draft, at this moment is £954.020 ; the bank overdraft is £62,119 ; but anyone who knows what business ia. a Corporation having enormous engagements. capital ex- penditure, biz sums required daily for the purchase cf properties and so forth, will think very little indeed of a bank overdraft amounting to £62,000. (Elem., hear.) I should like, however, on this to say a few thing that I think will be instructive. Ties private street work of the Corporation is becoming a very serious matter. The Corporation felt years age, and still feel, that it is a very serious hardship utter' owners of property to compel them, within & very few months, to pave and pay for the paving of their streets, almost immediately after tne erection of property. Hence it was decided some years ago that an owner of property might enter in a contract to pay for the street making in a period of three years by quarterly or half-yearly instalments, the amount boating interest at 4 per cent. We cannot borrow money in the ordinary way to pay for that, and consequently we treat that as part of the bank overdraft. It is pro— , fitable to us to do so. It pays its way. and consequently we are able to help the ratepayers, help the rateable value, without any cost to th 3 ratepayers, and £12,090 of that overdraft is practically standing on the private street making account,as part of the balance owing to the bank. There are various important works being done, the hospital extension, rolice build- ings the Bridge-streat widening, the construction of sewers, and the Technical Institute, for, which we are in a position to borrow the money, sanction having been obtained, but for which we still owe the bank. That amounts to £40,000 and at the first convenient moment we shall take up the moneys aril pay them to the bank so that that, need not in the slightest degree affect our indebtedness. There are various other sums being paid off,such as capital sums which we are paying off by the authority of the Council out of the revenue, these sums together with movable sums making up the disposable balance which a good tradesman always has or ought to have at his bankers. That is exactly the position of the Corporation, and we find it convenient, expedient and profitable to conduct our business in this way as indeed does every other first-class Corporation in the kingdom. I am obliged to you for your atten- tion and I think you will agree that the committee has been wise in offering to the Council as well RS to our correspondent the information that I have just given you. I only wish to say one other word. Our indebted- ness altogether Is £954,020 and £62,119, a total of £1,016,139, but if anyone of you will refer to the abstract of the accounts isaued by the Borough Treasurer for the 12 months ending March, 1902, you will find there that the Cornnration's actual assets on that date totalled up to £1,321,961, so that we had a surplus of assets at that time of £347,000 or about one-third of our entire indebted:teem These figures must only be very interesting, but it must be also very refreshing to feel that the Corporation is in such a sound financial poi- tier." (Applause.

' BUCKLEY-STREET P.S.A., WARRINGTON.—A PROTEST AGAINST SUNDAY TRAMS. ; There was a good attendance at an open meeting of ' the above P. 8.4. in Buckley-street 'Methodist Free ; Church on Sunday. The chair was oecupied by Wiliiam ' Smith. and the speaker was Mr Audrew Scriven. A . violin Rola was excellently rendered by Mr A Butcher, ° and Miss f. Fairhurst was heard to advantage in the ' solos " Where is heaven ? "and the " Volunteer Organ- jet," Mr Albert E Trow being the accompanist. —The Speaker, in basing his remarks upon " For every man shall bear his own burden," said in looking around upon the wretchedness and misery of the world, the question naturally arose why want and suffering were so prevalent ? The answer was to be found in the fact that every man had not borne his burden. Though they might call the Government " over the coals," though they might torture their town councillors with the fact of their deficiences, and though they might irritate the members of their Board of Guardians, even then they would not get to the source of the misery of the working classes, which was acting like a cancer upon the country. The great inroads which had been made upon the sacred- ness of the Sabbath day by divers concerns could and would have been stayed if their represestatives had stood up for the well-being of the working classes. He , thought the Sunday tram service would never have been I seen in this town if their Chi istrian representatives on 1 the Town Town Council had bad the courage to oppose I the diabolical scheme of making money "cheaply" on the Sabbath. 11 the tramways could not be made to pay without having to edge Sunday into the " working" week they ought never to have been introduced. When- ever they found people shirking the bearing of their burdens double burdens necessarily fell upon otbers,and thus while a few enriched themselves there were multi- itudes who had to expend an unnmessary amount of labour in order to maintain even a bare existsnee.—The C'naiernan proposed, Mr J J Fairhurst seconded, and it was unanimously resolv.d, that the following resolution should he sect to the Town Clerk :—" That this brotherhood of P S.A., meeting at Buckley-sr. Mntho- , dist Free Church, desires to enter its protest egainat the I running of trams on Sundays, which is.in their opinion, I detrimental to the welfare of the Christlon churches in Warrington, and trusts that the Town Council will de- cide, at an early date, to dispense with the Sunday i service of trams."

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY OCTOBER 10, 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY OCTOBER 10, 1902
TEMPERANCE MEETING AT WARRINGTON. Work for the Templars.

On Wednesday evening, a public meeting, under the auspices of the Temperance Mission Lodge of the 1.0.G.T. was held in the Ebenezer Mission Room, Buttermarket-stre 't. There Was a good audience, the members of the Order wearing their regalia. 4eMr Henry Thornton, J.P., presided, and he was sup- ported on the platform by Bro. the Rev J A Lee, D.C. r. Bro. F Merlic, C.T., Bro. J W Roberts. P.C.T., Bro. J Sheath, L.D., and Sister Miss Hampton,D.V.T., of East and Mid-Cheshire•—A letter of apology was received by I Bre- O'Brien, treasurer, who was on businets in Leeds. The meeting opened with the singing of " Stand up , for Jesus," after which prayer was led by Bro. Lee. A pianoforte solo as very wed eremted by Miss Elsie Johnson (who wore a. Coronation sash won by ber at Liverpool thi3 yoar.) The young artiste was loudly encored, and she oblieed with another solo. Miss Gerty Hughes rend-red a recitation entttld " Treating the men," with good effect. The CHAIR3IAN, after a few introduct.wy remarks,said that however illiterate a man or woman may be there was some work to do. The drinking habits Of this country were very bad. Here was 3 case in point. A girl, 15 years old was found lying drunk. Thank God she could not legally get drunk now. (Hear, hear). The publican who sold the liquor to the girl bad his license endorsed. It Was a pity he could not be endorsed. (Flear, hear). Could not something be done to stem the tile of intemperance in the land ? He gave some statistics to show the large amount of money spent in ' drink in this country. For every 24 spout in fond and clothing in this country, Is 61 was spent in drink, It Was a downright disgrace t too country (applause). ' An habitual drunkard—a woman who died in the begin- fling of this century—left 809 descendants. Of these, 1729 had died in prison and from the effects of drink, (Shame). This woman's descendants had cost the country no less than £26,000 through being in prison, workhouses, and asylums. Did they fully grasp the meaning of this sum ? Under present conditions, thou- sands of children were yearly born with an hereditary craving for drink. It remained for Good Ternplars and other societies to remedy this. He concluded by urging the members to go on with the good work they were crrrying on and God weul I bless them. (Applause). A few more musical items were then rendered. A gfei " Ringing cheerily," WAS well sung by the Templar Glee Party. Miss Minnie Broughton, a little tot of tour years old, recited " Little old women" so well that the audience demanded an encore which was • given. Miss 13 Bowyer delighted her hearer with an excellent , rendering of" Only Tired." She was accompanied on the piano by Miss Edith Leigh, who also reneered the contralto pait of the chorus. Bro J A ...aEE, D.O.T. then addressed the meeting. He WA3 pleased to be in Warrington and to congratulate the members of the lodge on their success during the past quarter. Lady Henry Somerset, a short time age, stated in the U.S.A. that she Was ashamed to tell the Americans that England had almost become a nation of drunkards, and it was hopeless to save her from the drink evil. He Was not so pessimiatic as that —(hear, hear)—temperance workers had much to be thankful for. During the last fifty ye ars,tenaperanee reform had traads great progress. The Chiliren's Bill had been passed thank God! It was now a great crime to send a young child for drink and that was something to rejoice for. (Hear, heat). But they were not satistied like Oliver Twist, they wanted more. They must not rest on their oars but pullagainst the stream. In his 22 years slum work in Liverpool, he had come across some awful cases of neglect and crime through drink. It the houses of the working-classes, he saw misery and buffer- iog from the effects of the drink curse. He had been told by the chairman that it was the same in Warring- ton ("Yes. ") Well, it was the duty of Good Ternplars to save the victims of this awful evil. Their motto was "to save the fallen and save others from falling." They must get the chil- dren into the juvenile temples, and train them in the principles of total abstinence—he was going to say temperance, but that was too broad a term. Let the Good Templars of Warrington act the part of Good Samaritans in their daily life and their reward would be assured. (Applause). A short time ago, he (the speaker) asked h Liverpool minister if he would start a lodge in connection with his church and he was told that good Templars' was dead. It was far from dead, it was very much alive. (Hear, hear). It could not die for the life of it. (Laughter and applause.) Last year in Eagland alone, there had been an increase of over 8,000 members. (Applause). In conclusion, he said that at a temper- ance demonstration he saw a short time ago, he noticed a banner which had on it the words, "All right now, daddy's !ober." It was all wrong in some homes and it was the bounden duty of all temperance reformers to do their level best to remedy this. (Loud applause). Miss Johnson tastefully gave another pianoforte solo and Mr C Nurse was heard to advantage in the render- ing of "Remember me, Almighty One " Bro J W ROBERTS moved and Bro F MERLIN seconded a hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman, speaker and artistes. This WAS carried with _acclamation and the meeting was closed by the singing of tbs Dexceogy and the pronouncing of the Beriedictioo. A number of pledges were;signed in the course of the evening.

div.head: REV. F. E. POWELL'S DEPARTURE,
div.p: THE REV. F. E. POWELL'S DEPARTURE,
Farewell Address.

A very large congregation assembled in St James' Church, Latchford, on Sunday evening, when the last of the services in connection with the harvest festival was held. At the close of the service the Rev F E Powell, who has now left the town to take up his duties as vicar of Sewerby. near Bridlington, delivered a farewell address. He said :—On this my last Sunday as vicar of St James', I desire to say a few simple words of affec- tionate farewell. It was at a harvest thanksgiving service, just four years ago, that I first stood in this pulpit, and preached to you my first sermon. Since then, in my short ministry among you, I have sought to enforce the lesson I then taught, that " man doth not live by bread alone," and have distributed among you that true bread that cometh down from heaven. This ministry among you, so imperfect and insufficient, so feebly and falteringly exercised, I now humbly and re- gretfully bring to an end. May .Goel pardon all that has been wrong and unworthy, may He bless the intention —and I call Him to witness to its reality and sincerity— to be of service to you in the great battle of life we are all cilled upon to fight Like our forefathers, we two are dwellers in tents. For a time, of more or less duration, we linger at some spot in life, we cultivate friendships, and I thank aod I have Icu ti rated many among you. For four years God has extended for me the day in which I was to work for Him at Latchford : my opening has at length come,my opportunity is at alas gone, and my work with all its shortcomings and failure., is done. In this month's Parish Magazine I have expressed my sincere thanks to those—whether named or unnamed—who have been friends and fellow workers in the noblest of all causes. There, too, you will find a reproof for those who ought have responded more to my appeals. Where I have failed I pray that your new vicar may succeed. For the sake of Christ and His Church, as well as ef yourselves, support Mr Pearson in all his undertakings for good. Pray for him, work with him, encourage him. You will lose nothing, but lain much if you do tbis,lor your new vicar is an earnest able parish priest of much personal charm and robust piety of life. Kindness and sympathy will flow. if you will allow it, in abundance from a surcharged heart, and it will not he long before you will respect and love him. Finally, my brethren.
farewell, Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind. live in peace; and ttio God of love and peace shall be with you. THANKS TO THE WARRINGTON CLERGY.

Speaking at a large gathering of Sunday school teachers and Warrington clergy in Holy Trinity School on Monday night, the Rev F E Pown,t, said he had never worked in any town where greater harmony pre- vai ed among Church people and among the clergy than in Warrington. (Applause.) His four years' stay in the town had been most helpful years indeed in that particu'ar if he were to mention no other. He was glad to have that opportunity of saying that his brother clergy had been most kind to him. It was with real regret that he went from Warrington, but there were compensating advantages in going away, for he hoped fcr better health for his family than they had had here. And there might be other compensating advantages. Eif, had assured his successor that among the Church people and clergy of Warrington he would receive a most eympathetic welcome,and that he would find him- self almost at once at home, just as he (Mr Powell) had done from the beginning to toe end. (Apn'ause.) PRESENTATION OF AN ADDRESS. FAREWELL MEETING.

Oa Mooday evening, the Rev F E Powell was the reci- pient of an address from the members of the congregation of St James', Latchford. The meeting at which the presentation was made took place in tho schoolroom and was largely attended. Mr N H Rou,ghton (vicar's warden) presided and he was sup/nevi on the platform by the Rev & N Taylor, and the following members of Church Council :—Messrs C S Burgess, T E Gibson, T Hutchinson Venn, Astley, Eekersley (people's warden), Fargher, Carruthers. Acton, Slater, and S'ansfiold (head schoolmasoer and secretary to the Church Council.) Each mornb 3r of he Church Council wore a button-hole, which had kindly been sent from Se werby, by Mrs

The CHAIRMAN expressed hi a reget at parting with Mr Pow:4l, and stited his appreciation of tan excellent work he had done in the parish. an said they had met that evening to wish him " God-speed," and the large number present ratified Co the regard they, a 3 parishi- oner ; felt for him.

!Ira making the presentation, Mr. C. SAWKINS BtruoEss eaid Mr Powell war leaving behind him a wel'-ergaoized and welt-equipped pariah, and Mr Pearson would find ready to band organizations which would materially help bin to carry on God's work in their ml at. (Applause.) Mr Powell had spared no effort to make the influence of trim religion felt in the lives and characters of those ! with whom became into contact and there were many who would look back upon his residence in Latchford with thankful hearts ; it would be a happy reflection for him that he left many behind who were the poorer for hie removal. He regretted that Mr 3 Powell w a not present, So that he might associate her with the few words of farewell he must say on their and his behalf. They all regretted their going, but above all, the cause of their departure. They sincerely hoped the change to a mare bracing climate would be bmeficial. Mr and Mrs Powell had during the four years of their residence in Latchford made many friendsoand he believed some of those friendships would list as long as they lived. They would miss mach Mr Powell'a counsel and help. He was a man of rnrnarkabie ability and extra- ordinary zeal,always fear:am and c mrageous in express- ing his convictions, and often by his strong personality and wonderlul force of character winning over his oppo- nents, who could but admire the pertinacity with vehici he clung to his views arid carried out. hl plans. Turning to Mr Poasell, Mr Bur,gesa said he had now the privilege , to present an address which read as follows :—" To the Rev Francis Edward Powell, MA. Dear Sir,—Toe members of the congregation of St James's, Latchford, having learnt witra regret that you are about to sever your connection with them, are desirous of expressing their appreciatioa of the wuk done by you during the last three years you have been amongst them. Your efforts for the moral, social, and in'ellectual advanae- meat of the people of the neighbourhood will long be remembered, while the Migsion Church of St Hilda, erected during your incumbency, remains a menu.nent to the zeal and energy you have displayed in all your undertakings for the welfare and airoverity of the parish. In bidding you • God-speed ' the metutiers of the congregation trust that yuur work at Fewerby will be abundantly ble,sed, and that, with renewed h and strength, you and Mrs Powell may belong spared to carry on the church's work ia thar parish.—Signed on behalf of the subscribers, HAMLET NEWHALL EIOLTGHTON, WILLIAM ECKEHSLEY, churchwardens, October 6tia, 1902."

The VICAR, in acitne wlidging the address, said that althongh he could hardly say he had blen t Oren b 7 sur- prise' he found it very difficult t 3 adequately express his very deep feelings in acknowledging the testimonial which ha i just been presented to him. Be did not, ot course, believe for nee moment that he deserved one of the all-too-kind words which Mr Burgess had spoken, but he thought his successor would go a long way towards meriting each high etoooniums. He might tell the parishioners that from the very outset he mule most careful inquiries concerning Mr Pearson, and he would certainly not have furthered this exchange had he not been eompletely satisfied. for he thought too much of his parishioners to leave them to be care of one even less efficient than himself. Of course, Mr Pearson was a high Churchman, as he hims, If was. Teat was they both thouekt very highlyof the Church mid her sacraments, and of that historic ceremonial which was the Church' lawful heritage. Tle could assure all his friends here that he parted from them with very real 'regret. He had !weed to value, respect, and love many hi connection with S. James', and they had been remarkably tolerant of him, for it must be remembered that he was a Social st Radical among Conser- vatives, a kind of pro-Boer in the midst of so-called Jingoes. Be desired to discount any implied offensiveness in the expressions—a teeto- taller among strictly moderate drinkers, and an anti-raft 1r among those who saw no particular harm in this form of speculation. He, on his part, had sought, too, to be perfectly tolerant, save to the intolerance of others and to what he was convinced was moral and social evil. He would regard that beautiful address— beautiful both in its design end kind words it expressed --as an indication of the friendly feeling they had ever shown him. They had been his friends and would con- tinue to be so. The address would often recall the times he bad spent in their midst. In no town in which he worked had he found greater harmony among the clergy and Church people as he load found in Warringtoo.Long might that happy condition of things continue. When he remembered the awful evils which stalked in their land he was perfectly amend that so much misdirected zeal and energy shonld have been thrown into the move- ment which was now disgracing the city o? Liverpool. Let them be tolerant ; at the same time hold noir con- viction !:rowdy. It was lack of conviction in matters pelitical and religions which Was the cause of so much indifference. Hs once more thanked all for their most kind feedings, which bai been al-t3e-generousiy ex- pre,sed by Mr Burgesi, He was above all so thankful to leave the congregation in such perfect harmony, net only with himsF lf but with one another. Might God's blessing rest upon them all. (Applause.) Tee Rev A N TAYLOR (curate) said the large congrega- tion assembled on Sunday night at church was a tribute to Mr Powell's work, for :all sections of thought :were th,ra represented—including many Dissenters and R nnan Ca'holics. Tney hoped it weul I not be a per marten': " Good bye," but hoped frequently to see the Vicar visiting Warrington and neighbourhood. (Hear. hear.)
to the clue of

Mr ECRERSLE? (people's warden) and Alderman HUTCHINSON also spoke. T E GIBSON in moving a vote of thanks to the Chairman and to Mr Burgess, said that Mr Powell, since he came four short years ago, by his marked rersonality his wide range of thought and reading, and his eloquent power of expussion by voice and pen had won the high esteem of people outside his own parish, and, in many instances differing from him pa opinion, No one could charge him either with intolerance of other peo?le's belief, or of lack of courage in defending his own. M, STANSFIELD in seconding, also expressed his regra at Mr Powell's departure. Be might remind them that during Mr Powell' term of office as Vicar, he had raised no less a sum then an average of £6OO a year, aid that had heen done without the aid of h •zaarsoka. They all regretted especially the cause for which Use Vicar W.IS leaving them. Had he been going on promotion—had he been leaving to become a bishop for instance—they would have parted with him with leas regret, but when they considered that Mrs Powell' health necessittee that change, they all regretted this cause and hoped the change would be beneficial to Ire Powell and a happy one for all the family. (Applauae). Mr POWELL SlippOrtel the vote of thanks, which was Carried unanimously, and the meeting terminatea with the 13!e, slog pronounced by the Vicar.

Local Prize Winners at the Dairy Shows"! ' Among the prize winners in the poultry classes at the dairy show now being held at the Agricul- tural Hall, London, we notice that Mr E Burrow, Warrington, obtained a second prize for Working homer cock that has fiswn 200 miles, and a first for working homer cock that has flown over one hundred miles. Mr H G Johnson, of Earlestown, gained a first and cup for a short-faced tumbler I bred in 1902. Warrington Athletic Club. The weekly cross-country run of this Club took place from headquarters, the Bridge Inn, on Saturday last. The hares, ei Price and A Ford were despatched with the paper at 3.30 p.m., the pack, which was composed of 16 runners, turning out 15 minutes later, H Kean acting as pace and J Mather (captain) whipper in. The hares laid the trail over the usual club course, through Arpley fields over Walton Arches, and then across the fields to Bobs Bridge. From here the course was along the canal bank and across country to Moore. From this point the route was along the Ship Canal and the Railway to the New Road, where the pack lined up for a break to headquarters The first to arrive was C Straw, followed by C Dagnall, H Hill third, and R Price fourth. The run, a distance of 7 miles, occupied 50 minutes. TABLB & HANGING LANIPS.—L. S. CIAttLAND, 51, k 55 Bridge-street, IN arrhagtori.—Advt.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held at Bewsey Chambers on Wednesday afternoon. There were present !—Messra T Halton (in the chair), Knowles Brooks, Houghton, Forshaw. Backhouse and Dr Murray, with Dr Sephton (medical officer of health), Messrs J C Sutton (clerk), 8 Sutton (assistant clerk), F Kerfoot (inspector of nuisances), B S Newcombe (surveyor), and H H Burnage (assistant surveyor).

div.head: COMPLAINTS FROM BURTON WOOD.
div.p: COMPLAINTS FROM BURTON WOOD.

The following letter has been received from Mr John Fairclough, Clerk to the Burtonwood Parish Council " Dear Sir,—Complaints having been made to the Council of the dangerous position lot several telegraph posts in Phipps-lane and Penny-,ana, lam to request that you will instruct your Surveyor to apply to the proper authorities for a removal ot the danger. lam also to point out to your Inspector the unsatisfactory candition of the brook at IThipp's Bridge." Mr Feminism said that some of the telegraph posts at Collins Green were right in the centre of bs path. Mr KNoWLES called attention to the posts alongside the wall of Winwick Asylum. He said they we.e erected ten or twelve years ago when the traffie was not a quar- ter of what it was to-day. In consequence of the pre- sent enormous traffic the posts were very dangerous. The SURVEYOR was asked to write to the Post Office authorities requesti:eiz them to remove the posts at 1 Winwick and Codins Green.

With regard to the brook at,Burtonwood the Inspector said the matter had been before the Council several time.. Mr Forshaw had pet down a most extensive sewerage scheme at the brewery but at times it did not appear to work as it should do, The Cumarktnu said he thought Mr For3laaw had done as much as he c uald in the meter.

Dr SEPETON said he saw the brook about ten days itgo and there was nothing to complain of. From what ho had heard the preEeot condition of the brook was caused by barm bring turned down the cower. It wag decided that the medical officer sh-aild inspect • brook ana see if he could suggest anything to improve its condition.

THE BOLD MORTUARY QUESTION. Further correspondence wica Mr E Peace, solicitor, , Liverpool, upon this question was submitted by the I cletk. Oa September 12clo iu reply to a letter from Mr Sutton conveying the C-algell'H views oa the matter, Mr Peace wrote :—Dear Sir,—l am obliged by yours of yesterday's date. lam sorry if I did net make myself clear in my letter to you upon this matter. lam in- structed that there is no mortuary for the township of Burtonwooci which also applies to the township of Bold and in the ordinary course of events I should be com- pelled to urge open each township the necessity of pro- viding a mortuary, but having regard, however, to my conversation with Mr 13righouse, his Mijesty's Coroner, he is agreeable if the two toy:whips con agree between themselves that one mortuary should suffice for both townships. I shall ho pleased to hear further from you before takmg up the matter with the Local Government Board. _ _

In reply the Clerk wro%:. :—" Der sir. The Cotricil think that the provision by th 3 overseers of Burtonwood is sufficient. Tne ne3essity for a mortuary seems to arise at Bold, a towaship wholly within the district of the Whiston Rural District Council. Under these cir— cumstances the Whigon C-Aalcil was th 3 proper author- ity to (deal with the subject of your letter." Mr Pearce then wrote stating that his client would b 3 glad to know what provisions if any hid been made by the overse,rs of Burtonwood.—Th Cl,rk replied explaining that the overseers of Burtonwood had an arrangement to pay the publicans of the di.trict to provide rooms for the few cases that arose. Mr Peace formally acknowledged this letter.
The Clerk said ti 3 wal how the nnttn stood at pre- sent. Pracically i d fficutr.s, wri.097,-,e ex Burtonwood, that township being proviio I f by th overseers.
THE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT-OUTBREAK OF ENTERIC FEVER AT WINNVIBK ASYLLTIK. .

Dr Seeztamer reported that during the month there had been 17 births and 25 deaths. Tie death rate was equal to 26 per 1,000 against 25, toe average of the last three moons and 99 for the corresponding mouth of last year. &can the last meeting of the Council an outbreak of enteric fever had occurred at the County Asylum Winwick. Sixteen cases had been reported, five of which Droved fatal. He suspected the milk as the factor in these cases, caused by the cows having grazed on a pasture over which sEwage had "flu wn " A sample of milk, water, and the effluent from the sewage was sent for examination and Professor Boyce reported that he had found no typhoid bacilli either in the milk or water, but in the milk he had found a large number of bacillus colt and in the water bacillus coli communis, and he regarded both the water and the milk as a goatee of danger. He (Dr Sephton) had reported the outbreaks both to the Local Government Board and to the County C Duncil. The first case was noticed on tha 14th of September and the last case on the 28:h. &xteen of the 25 deaths reported occurred at the Win. wick Asylum and exclusiva of these the death rate was 8.6 per 1,000. Dr Sephton also informed the Conned that Dr Simpson had the matter in band and had wtitten to him stating that other samples would be taken for analy43, to endeavour to detect the cause of intection. Dr Sephton added that the milk and the water were now being 11;ileil before use and certain sanitary arrangr- ments of a minor character were being improved, He thought that the mills might have got contaminated by sewage water and in all probability some sewage had found its way into the water pipes which supplied the asylum. The INSPECTOR Said that samplea of water had been taken from the pipes at Winwiek which did not supply the asylum, and they w mid be analysed. The ASSISTANT CLERK said DT Simpson had told him that they never had an asylum built without an epi- demic of typhoid breaking out soon after the occupation of the building. The report was adopted. THE S3IITTI LANCASHIRE TRANWAYS-IHE NEWTON TO

WARRINGTON SECTION. The SURVEYOR reported the receipt of the following lstter dated October 7th from Yr Alfred Tracer, secre- tary tci th 3 South Lancashire Tramways Company, in reply to a communication asking for information with regard to the date of the commence Lent of the proposed service ht wen Newton and Warrington :—Dear Sir,— Your letter of the 22nd ult., was: brought before the direotors of the Board meeting held yesterday, and I have to inform you that the construction of the tram- ways from Newton to Warrington hag the serious con- sideration of the Board, who are anxious to put into effect all the powers of the company as early as possible, and although the section referred to will be dealt with as soon as practicable, it le Impossible at present to give even an approximate date when this is likely to he done. I regr.t that I am unable to write you more definitely, but when I am in a position to do so 1 will again , communicate with you."
POULTON LIGHTING AND WATER SUPPLY.

The INRPECTOR reprted that the committee appointed to fix the site for gas lamps at Poulton-witb-Fearn'ioad met,on the 19% September. It was decided to erect eight 13rar)9 in Manchester-road. Poulton, and one in Manchester-road, Woolston, just outside the boundary of Poulton, also two lamps in Cinnamon-lane, Feat head. The Clerk had given the necessary order for the lamps to be ereermd and the work would be proceeded with at once.—There was a scarcity of good water to property situate at Manchester-road, Poulton. The Csrporation water main was close at hand and he pro- posed asking the Water Engineer upon what terms and conditions the water would be supplied. This was all the business of pubic interest.

div.head: SEQUEL TO AN ACCIDENT AT VULCAN FOUNDRY. Compensation Claim.
div.p: SEQUEL TO AN ACCIDENT AT VULCAN FOUNDRY. Compensation Claim.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday be- fore His Honour Judge Bowan Rowlands, a claim under the Workmen's Compensation Act was heard in which Hecry Andrew, living at 34, Manchester- row, Vulcan, Earlestown was the applicant and the Vulcan Foundry Company, Earlestown, the re- spondents. Mr A Browne, Warrington,represented the applicant and Mr Cobbett, Manchester, the ro4pondents. . .

Mr A Browne, in opening the case, said the applicant was employed as a driller by the Vulcan Foundr3 Com- pany, and in June last he was seriously iniated on the hand whilst following his employment. The respondents continued to pay applicant 103 21 a week, which was half his average earnings, up to the 4th of July. On , that date the money was stopped owing to the respond- ' ent haying asked the firm to fils an agreement as to compensation in the County.,Court. The applicant was very seriously injured as ho was now unable to grip the tools which he used in his employment.—. Beery Andrew informed the Court that on the day of the accident be was drilling frames for locomot vs when an accident caused him to lose the first joint of the first finger the two first joints cf the second finger and a portion of the third finger of the lett hand, Be received 108 2d from the firm, which was half his wages, up to the 4th July. Ia the course of his work he had to handle a machine and use a chisel, a centre punch, a hamer and other tnol4. The injury had incapacitated him from beirm able to follow his employment as he was unable to grip the tools. At the request of the firm, his injuries were examined by Dr Mounsey and in consequence of what the doctor told him he had not been to the works.
In answer to bis Honcur, Mr Brown said the claim now made was for half the appliclot's wages for the past eleven weeks, £5 lls and for an order for future payments on a similar scale.

Cross-exammed by Mr Cobbett, the applicant said he had never attempted 0 work since the accident. He was wining to do so if the case were adj3urned. It was decided t adjourn the ease to December 4th in order that the applicant might endeavour to resume work. the rerpondents to afford every facility for his doing so.

div.head: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
The Supply of Electricity.

A meeting of the Urban District Council of Newton- in•Makerfield was held in the Town Hall, Earhstown, on Monday evening. Mr J W Calling wood presidei and there were also present : Dr. Patteraon, Dr. Latham Messrs. C B F Barron, C.C., J. W. Emmett, J.P., T Ormand, N Siddeley, J Simpson, W Gilmour, W Thomp- wu, L B,mt,E T Evane with W C Cale (clerk),l Bowes (surveyor), R T Surtees (gas-engineer).
THE TECEINICAL INSTRUCTION SPECIAL GRANT.

Toe Cl-rk haviag reported to the Tchnical Instruc- tion Committee that the amount (L 75 allotted to this district nut of the special grant of £2,000 voted by the County Council to Urban District for special purposes, had been paid to the treasurer. It was resolv3d that the Financt Committee be recimmended to pass a chequs in favour of the Viaduct InstVute Technical Instruction Committee for the sum of £75.
The recommendation was agreed to on the proposition of Dr Paterson. DR. LATIUM AND DEFICIENT GAS LIGHTING.

At a meeting of the Gas Committee the Engineer reported with respect to the provision of additional lamps for lighting the following streets, 17iz. :—Birch. street, Cherry-street, Clarence-Areet, Neville-street, SchoW-street, Foundry-street, Water-street,Hydai-street It was proposed by Councillor Boum, and seconded by Councillor Giimour, that the report be referred back to the Engineer with instructions to prepare a full report of the additional lamps required for the whole of the district, and to sunply a copy of such report to each member of the Committee price to the next meeting. It was then proposed by Councillor Latham and seconded by Councillor Emmett, as an amendment, that the Engineer's report be received and adopted and that the Engineer be directed to proceed with the work. On the amendment being put to the meeting, four members of tno Com- mittee voted for and five against the same, and it was declared lost. rho original :notion was then put and carried, Councillors Emmett and Latham only voting against the same. A letter was read from the trustees of the Wesleyan Church, asking the C)mrnittee to con- siclrr the question of the hetter lighting of the side street leading off Crors-lane to School-street, and applying for a lamp to be placed near to the gateway leading into the Lecture Hall.—lt was resolved that the Engineer be directed to carry out the standing resolution of the Committee with respect to the lighting of plac's of pub- lic worship. A. letter was also read from Mr S Harvey, on behalf of the minister and deacons of the Earlestown Baptist Church, suggesting that the lamp in Crown- street should be moved to the corner by the main entrance to the Churcli.—lt was resolved that the Engineer be directed to consider the matter when pre- paring his rep -)rt upon street lighting. Mr Thompson moved the confirmation of the minutes. Dr Latham referred to the lighting question and said It was absolutely necessary that the streets meotioned in the list shoull be lighted at once. Most of them, he said, were new streets and with the exception of two, no lights weatever were provided. Rs also pointed nut that Acacia-street and Lyme-street were also without lights. Dr Lal ham was proceeding to enlarge upon this subject when Mr Ormand said he wished to know whether this was an amendment within the meaning of the stand- ing orders. Be (Mr Ormsnd) thought it was nor. From Dr Latham's lengthy speech he failed to see that it was an amendment within the meaning of the standing orders. _ . . .

The Chairman said it seerriPd to be going over the same ground again and it would be better to stick to the principle and spirit of the standing orders. Hs ruled Dr Latham out of order,but he thought Dr Latham would be in Order if he proposed that the minute be re- ferred back. _ _
Dr Latham : I think I am entitled to defend my rips.tion before you give your rulinz. Mr Orman I: I a•iked for the Chairman's ruling. I did not ask for Dr L arliam's .

Dr Litharn : I say the Chairman is wrong if he rules the anyndrnent out of order. Ith Gilmour : I say Dr Latham is out of order. He ought to have given notic,. Ir Ormand : Then I say we have placed W. Colin,.;- wood in the chair with every clofidence iu his ability land imptrialitv to conduct the bußiness,and when atIF member a.opetls t ) him tor his deeisbn nom the m att6 r of debate we ought to take his decision and submit to it. If we think be is wrong then we can toll him so privately. Dr Latham : I would like to know, if a member i 3 not entitled to que,ttoo the raising of a point of order ? _ . .
Oemu : Not if the) ChaimAn ssys you ate out of order. . .
Dr Latham : I say lam entithd. I say the Chair- man's decision is entirely at variance with the standing orders. It is not the first either. The minutes were then !passed. "WATER COMMITTEE.

At a meeting held on the 16th Septernter, it 9739 re- solved that th 3 Chairman kid the Engmeer be em- powered to make arrangements with Mr Poole (the contractor for the sinklne, of the additional well) Er the lowering of the pumps in the boreholes, that the water therein will not ba affect3l by the sinking operations in connection with the new well. It was also resolved that the coatractor (Mr J J Poole) be offered the sum of £25 to lower the pumps in the two boreholes a distance of 24 feet, and to fit them up into go 3cil working order again, within 12 days from the date of the order to commence the work ; and chat if he accepts such offer, the Council allow him a premium of £2 104 for every day under the stipulated time in which the work is corn - plated, and that the Chairman of the Water Corrnmittee and Councillors Collingwood and Wood be appointed a deputation to wait upon Mr F W Webb, engineer to the London and North-western Railway Comany, Crewe, with the view of obtaining his sanction to such tem- porary supplies of water as may be required by the inhabitants during the present shaking of the additional well. The minutes were approved on the proposition of hit Barron.

HIGHWAYS AND SANITARY COMMITTEE, At a meeting of this Committee it was resolved that the bui!ding plan submitted by Mr William John Pat (Warrington), for the erection of a 1101120 and shop co en- bined at the corner of Cherry-s,reet and Ly rne-itr tet be approvod. The Committee reconsidered the question of the advisability of obtaining a provisional order with rerpnc:t to the provision of a water carriage syst om for all new property, when it was proposed by Council )r Gilmour, and seconded by Counoillor B3rron, that the previous minutes upon the question be deleted. Pro- posed by Councillor Evans, and seconded by CJuncillor Patterson as an amendment, that the Council be re- commended to apply for a Provisional Order. Jo the amendment bring put three members of the Committee voted for and five against the same, roil it was declared lost. The original motion was then put and carried. These minutes wero passed on the propositiou of the Chairman.
THE SUPPLY OF ELECTRICITY.-PROVISIONAL ORDER TO BE APPLIED FOR.

The Clerk reported to the General Purposes Committee it a meeting held on Monday aftornoon that he was of o- pinion that the notice:which ha I been received from the ProvinciallElectrie Supply and Traction Company of tin ir intention to apply to the Board of Trade for a provi- Biota/it order authorising them to supply electricity for any public or private purpsses within this district, was invalid unless the Council resolved to treat it as other- wise, ihe notice not having been serve I in accordance With the Board of Trade rules. He also informed the committee that tho solicitors to the company had informed him that they intended proceeding with the proposed application. It was resolved that the Council be recommended to oppose till application when made to the Board of Trade. The Clerk also reported to the committee that the Lancashire Electric Power Comoany obtained Parlia- mentary powers in the session of 1900 for the supply of eleotriticurrent in bulk to local anthorP.'es inLancashire, south of the Ribble and that the company would be prepared to negotiate with the Council,for the supply to them cf current In bulk on the Council obtaining the necesiory provisional order, to empower them to dis- tribute electricity. It was resolved that the Council be recommended to apply to the Board of Trade for a provisional order under the? Fllec:ric Lighting Acts 1832-83 authorising them to supply electricity f( r any public or private purposes within the district.
The minutes were agreed to. INCREASE OF SALARIES.

Mr Ormand,in moving the confirmati m of the minutes of the Staff Committee, stated that the Clerk's salary now recommended hid been unanimoualy approved by the Finance emmittee. The recommendation wks that the Clerk's salary be increased from £2OO to £250 per annum and that on the 29th Sept. 1903, it be mereased to £275, and that on the 29th September, 1904, it be further increased to £3OO. It was also recommended that the salary of Mr W Gorse, clerk is the co'lactor's department, be increased from £lOO to £llO per annum. The minutes were unanimously agreed to.

The Clerk said he would like to take that opoortunity of expressing his sincere thanks for the kind considera- tion the members had shown to him. Ft gave him extreme gratification to know that the Council valued his services so much, and he would always endeavour to deserve that appreciation in the future. (llear,hear).

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
Trades Council Application to Visit the House Refused.

A meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held in the Board Room at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Dr Patterson presided, and there were also preen nt :—Mrs Clay, Rev Father Wilson, Dr Murray, Messrs A J Jolley, T 11 Ashcroft, J Billinge, S Davies, William Hickman,A Brocks,A Jolley, William Houghton, J tiackhouse, G Piling, J Robinson. R Forshaw, J ninon E L Bent, T Halton, J W Knowles, with J Sutton (clerk), and F Gate ( workhouse master). HOUSE COMMITTEE. At a meeting held on the 1911 September, it was recommended that E Hewitt (37) be appointed non- resident night porter and stoker, at a weekly wage of 259, subject to deduction under the Poor Law Officees' Superanuation Act. This is instead of a resident night porter and stokrr.—lt was recommended that J W Dau-- man, aged 24 years, be appointed hospital porter at a salary ci! £25 per annum with rations, uniform, and washing.—At a meeting held on September 26th, it was recommended that Mr Miller, Liverpool, be asked to say what his charge would be tor teeting the new electrical work.—At a meeting on October 3r3 it was recommend- ed tnat the Master communicate with the Borough Electrical Engineer respeeting the testing of the new work executed at the woskhouse by Messrs E Morton and Company.—lt was recommended that Miss Mary Milner,ofSkipton,and Miss Lucy Delahay, of Croft, be appointed probationer nurses at salaries of £l2 first ! year, £l6 second year, and £2O third year with rations, uniform, and washing, Toe minutes w-re approaed on the motion of Mr BROOKS, seconded by Mr Purairtei. THE AMENDED DIETARY TABLES. 'The assistant secretary of the Local Government Board wrote acknowlo.ging the receipt of the Clerk's t-,er requesting the Board's sanction to amended dietary tanles which the Guardians of the Warri.gton Union have adopted for use at the Workhouse. He was directed to state that assuming the regulations in the Board's order of the 10th October,l9oo have been duly complied with,the sanction of the Board was not needed to the amended table,' submitted. THE EARLESTOWN TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL. APPLICATION TO VISIT THE HOUSE REFUSED.

The CLERK read the following letter :—" Park-road, Newton-le-Willows, 9th September. The Board of Guar- dians, Warrington. Gentlemen,—The Earlestown Trades and Labour Council have for some time had under CDR • sideration the question of old age pensions and the workhouse system, and whether any amelioration of the latter is immediately possible. Rio writer has just spent a fortnight in Dimmark where. under the guidance ef Alderman Klausen, M.P., of Copenhagen, he has been afforded an opportunity r f investigating on the spot the conditions of both the Old Age Pension Homes and the Work:oases. Both these institutions are open for the inspection of visitors any day. Tne Earlestown Trades Council is of opinion that the same privilege might b 3 etrended, if not to the pubic yet at least to certain representative public bodies, and I have to r:luest your Board to be so good ae to grant to myself and co-dele- gate the privilege of visiting occasionally the Workhouse at Warrington. A little consider stion will show that of all public bodies none are more directly interested in the humane and generous administration of the Workhouse than direct representatives of labour such as Trades Councils. I can assure you that the privilege we ask for will be judiciodsly and sparingly used, and that due care will be taken to cause no inconvenience to any o the officials of the Workhouse—Your obedient servant, WiLttem SPEAKMAN, hon. secretary, Earlestown Trades and Labour Council.

The CLERK added that he had written to the secre- tary to the effect that he knew of no authority possessed by Boards of Guardians ;authorizing the appointment of committees of the hind suggested to visit workhouses. There was an ordir with regard to women which was put in force in the Warrington Union. Mr KNOWLES proposed that the letter " lie on the table." Mr GEORGE PILLING seconded. Mr BENT : I will make inquiries as to who the Chairman of the Trades Council I don't see why we should stand out if we can give them the privilege. Mr ALFRED JOLLEY : The Warrington Trades Council tried the same thing on and were refused. Dr PATTER9ON : A similar application was made to the Wigan Union. Mr BENT: It makes people think there is something THE ESTIMATES. we want to keep in the dark. Mr BENT asked for some explatatiort as to the cause of the increase in the estimates fcr the ensuing ids months. 'rho Crs. : it was explained in the eslimate3 sent to you. MrBENT : I see the increase with. regard to the schools comes to £l5O.

The CLERK : &cause the schools are very full. We have to provide enough money. I am afraid our balance in the hands of the treasurer, which is nearly £2,000 less than it was 12 months ago, will hardly see me through. I shall have to ask the overseers to pay their contributions at the earliest possible date. The expenditure of the Union is going on very materially. Mr BENT referred to the increased expenditure at Newton, and asked whether the new offices were respon- sible for it.

The CLERK replied that the cost of maintaining the new buildings would be much more than the rent which was formerly paid for the use of an office at Newton. This was all the business of public interest.

Practical Charity.—A Chance for the Benevolent. ---- Sir,—Praetical charity is still an active force la this much-abused town of Warrington, ad the Press is mighty to direct its efforts. On the 4):12 inst the local newspapers announced the fast that a sum of money turd been sent to me for Alfred Harrison, the cripple who saved a lad from drowning. The lady who sent the money obtained her knowledge of the brave deed from a London Journal which had doairt• loss copied the item from the newspapers of this district. No sooner had the lady's munificence been chronicled in the Warrington Press than I received an offer from Mr Spann, a iocal coach-builder, to present Harrison with • cart suitable for the greengrocery trade. The offer was accompanied by a suggestion that some equally sheet- able resident ot our town might, of his bounty, furnish the cart's motive power in the shape of a little horse, or that Harrison might be supplied with the means of 'procuring one. Wherefore I repeat that the Press is a mighty organ and that Practical Charity is a living thing amongst us. —Faithfully yours, LIMB TkLBOT (Chief Constable).

They will rejoin the Renown at Suez and proceed direct to Bombay, calling only at Aden to coal. They are due at Bombay about Christmas day and will proceed direct to Delhi by train for the great durbar. After this they will pay various visits in India; and they are not expected home until March. Their suite will con- sist of Colonel and Mrs. Bingham, Mrs. Clayton. and Colonel Jarvis. There are at present many rumours of probable trouble in Northern Nigeria where the Sultan of Sokoto and the Emirs of Kano and Gando rule powerful and hitherto unconquered countries. The last named emir has recently professed friend- ship for us and has promised to assist the British Commissioners, Colonel Elliot and Lieutenants Foulkes and Frith, all of the Royal Engineers, who sailed on Saturday last from Liverpool to meet the French Commissioners and settle the vexed question of the exact boundary of our sphere of influence and theirs. This can hardly be acecm- plished if those three Hausa chiefs prove unfriendly: and the outcome of the Commission may mean trouble. The Emir of Kano has already been endeavouring to stir up trouble and to alienate the goodwill of the Chief of Zaria : and, as a pre- cautionary measure, three hundred men have already been sent up to reinforce Captain Abadie, the British resident.
